metadata.title: source paper of the fpvandoorn/carleson blueprint

extraction_notes.note: Hardy-Littlewood proposition marked external (the paper calls it a 'classical Vitali covering result and maximal function estimate', uncited); it is re-proved in Section 9, that proof is paper.
Introduction: results of Stein-Wainger, Lie, Zorin-Kranich and others are only mentioned (no statement in full) and get no nodes; acknowledgement text skipped.

The proof of the partial Fourier sum bound cites \eqref{g-small}, a label in the later lemma partial-Fourier-sums-of-small; the identical hypothesis of the lemma being proved is unlabelled. The ref edge from the later equation is kept as stated.
Lemmas whose proof is only 'This is part of the Lean library' are marked origin external (standard library facts), though the paper states them as its own lemmas.
claim or remark: the paragraph concluding that (R, rho, mu, 4) is doubling from the preceding lemmas is kept as a claim because the proof of real Carleson relies on it.

Sentences in Sections 3 and 4 that restate the standing setup of Section 2 ('Let $(X,\rho,\mu,a)$ be a doubling metric measure space ...', 'Let a measurable function $Q$ with finite range be given.', the recalled definition of $S$) get no node: they repeat definitions given in Section 2.

The uniqueness of the minimal parent cube $J$ is asserted and argued inline inside the recursive definition of $\Omega$; extracted as a claim ending at the colon plus a prose proof, both nested in the definition.
The adjoint T^*_p used in the statement of tile-correlation is only written out inside the proof of dens1-antichain (eq-tstarwritten); a term edge from that nested equation was added.

The tile set $\mathfrak S$ is defined inside the proof of the correlation separated trees lemma (equation def-Tree-S-set) but used in the statements of the following lemmas; kept as an equation nested in that proof with term edges to its users.
The sentence 'Recall that B(J) := B(c(J), 8D^{s(J)})' (Sec. 7.5.2) only recalls the earlier definition of B(J); no node was made for the recalled copy.

Sec. 7.6 redefines J' ('note that this is different from the J' defined in the previous subsection'); the Sec. 7.5 lemmas use the earlier J', the Sec. 7.6 lemmas this one, and term edges were drawn accordingly.
Standing 'fix a, X, K for the remainder of this chapter' sentence emitted as an assumption node (could be a definition); linked to the chapter's lemmas with inferred edges.
'Note:' about a stronger formalization of Hardy--Littlewood (unbounded w, applied to T_r g) emitted as a remark; it records a Lean-formalization detail rather than mathematics proper.

The proof of the weak (1,1) theorem starts in prose before the four auxiliary lemmas (trivial case, then the CZ setup) and resumes in the [Proof of] environment; the trivial case is a separate proof part, and the setup sentences that introduce c, g, b, B_{3,j}, B_{6,j}, Omega (used by the lemmas) are definition nodes.

metadata.extraction_comment: Extracted in ten source-range parts and merged; the cross-part term edges from the Section 2 standing definitions were added at merge from the finishing step's defined-term warnings, uniformly at confidence 0.75.

nodes.name: trigonometric polynomial
nodes.statement_short: A trigonometric polynomial $s_N(x)=\sum_{n=-N}^N c_n e^{inx}$.

nodes.name: trigonometric polynomial $s_N$
nodes.statement: s_N(x):= \sum_{n=-N}^N c_n e^{inx} \ .
nodes.label: eq:trig-series

nodes.name: Fourier series
nodes.statement:
The Fourier series is then defined as the limit $f$
of such a sequence $s_N$ as $N$ tends to $\infty$.

nodes.name: Fourier coefficients (Fourier integral formula)
nodes.statement:
The first question has a fairly canonical and standard answer, provided by the Fourier integral formula:
\begin{equation} c_n:=\widehat{f}_n:=\frac 1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(x) e^{- i nx}\, dx,
\end{equation}
 where the precise interpretation of the integral depends on the chosen theory of integration.
nodes.statement_short: Fourier coefficients $c_n=\widehat f_n=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(x)e^{-inx}dx$.

nodes.name: Fourier integral formula
nodes.statement: c_n:=\widehat{f}_n:=\frac 1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(x) e^{- i nx}\, dx,
nodes.label: eq:fourier-coefficients

nodes.name: Luzin's conjecture
nodes.statement:
Such convergence
was conjectured by N. Luzin \cite{Luzin13}
for the space
$L^2(0,2\pi)$, see also the collected works \cite{Luzin53}.
nodes.statement_short: Fourier series of $L^2(0,2\pi)$ functions converge almost everywhere.

nodes.name: Kolmogorov's example
nodes.statement: Kolmogorov's example \cite{Kolmogorov} of an $L^1$ function whose Fourier series diverges at almost every point seemed to provide some evidence against Luzin's conjecture.
nodes.statement_short: There is an $L^1$ function whose Fourier series diverges almost everywhere.
conclusions: an $L^1$ function whose Fourier series diverges at almost every point

nodes.name: Carleson's theorem (classical Carleson)
assumptions: Let $f$ be a $2\pi$-periodic complex-valued continuous function on $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fourier series of a continuous $2\pi$-periodic function converge to it almost everywhere.
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a $2\pi$-periodic complex-valued continuous function on $\mathbb{R}$. Then for almost all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ we have \begin{equation} \lim_{N\to\infty}s_N f(x) = f(x), \end{equation} where $S_N f$ is the $N$-th partial Fourier sum of $f$ defined in \eqref{eq:trig-series} with coefficients \eqref{eq:fourier-coefficients}.
nodes.label: classical-carleson

nodes.name: almost everywhere convergence of partial Fourier sums
nodes.statement: \lim_{N\to\infty}s_N f(x) = f(x),
nodes.label: eq:fourier-limit

nodes.name: Hunt's theorem
nodes.statement:
Shortly after Carleson's breakthrough, Hunt \cite{MR238019} proved the analogous result for $L^p$ functions
with $p>1$ and for functions in $L^1\log(L)^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Almost everywhere convergence of Fourier series for $L^p$, $p>1$, and $L^1\log(L)^2$.

nodes.name: Billard's theorem (Walsh-Fourier series)
nodes.statement:
Billard \cite{MR217510} adapted Carleson's arguments to prove almost everywhere convergence of Walsh-Fourier series
for functions in $L^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Walsh-Fourier series of $L^2$ functions converge almost everywhere.
conclusions: almost everywhere convergence of Walsh-Fourier series

nodes.name: Carleson's operator
nodes.statement:
In \cite{fefferman}, C. Fefferman gave an alternative proof of Carleson's theorem via an a priori
bound for Carleson's operator, the maximally modulated singular integral
\begin{equation} Tf(x):=\sup_{N} \int_{-\pi}^\pi e^{iNy}f(x-y)\frac 1y {dy}\, .
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Carleson's operator $Tf(x)=\sup_N\int e^{iNy}f(x-y)\frac{dy}{y}$; Fefferman's alternative proof bounds it.

nodes.name: Carleson's operator
nodes.statement: Tf(x):=\sup_{N} \int_{-\pi}^\pi e^{iNy}f(x-y)\frac 1y {dy}\, .
nodes.label: eq:feffermancarleson

nodes.name: doubling metric measure space
nodes.statement:
A doubling metric measure space $(X,\rho,\mu, a)$ is a complete
and locally compact metric space $(X,\rho)$
equipped with a non-zero locally finite Borel measure $\mu$ that satisfies the doubling condition that for all $x\in X$ and all $R>0$ we have
\begin{equation} \mu(B(x,2R))\le 2^a\mu(B(x,R))\,,
\end{equation}
where we have denoted by $B(x,R)$ the open ball of radius $R$ centered at $x$:
\begin{equation} B(x,R):=\{y\in X: \rho(x,y)<R\}. \end{equation}
nodes.genus:
complete
and locally compact metric space $(X,\rho)$
differentia: equipped with a non-zero locally finite Borel measure $\mu$ that satisfies the doubling condition
nodes.statement_short: A complete locally compact metric space with a Borel measure satisfying $\mu(B(x,2R))\le 2^a\mu(B(x,R))$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Statement of the metric space Carleson theorems

nodes.name: doubling condition
nodes.statement: \mu(B(x,2R))\le 2^a\mu(B(x,R))\,,
nodes.section: 1.1 Statement of the metric space Carleson theorems
nodes.label: doublingx

nodes.name: open ball $B(x,R)$
nodes.statement: B(x,R):=\{y\in X: \rho(x,y)<R\}.
nodes.section: 1.1 Statement of the metric space Carleson theorems
nodes.label: eq-define-ball

nodes.name: closed balls compact, measure positive on open sets
nodes.statement: In a doubling metric measure space the closed balls are compact and $\mu$ is positive on all non-empty open sets.
assumptions: In a doubling metric measure space
conclusions: $\mu$ is positive on all non-empty open sets

nodes.name: compatible collection of functions
nodes.statement:
A collection ${\Theta}$ of real valued continuous functions on the doubling metric measure space $(X,\rho,\mu,a)$ is called compatible,
if there is a point $o\in X$ where all the functions are equal to $0$,
and if there exists for each ball $B \subset X$ a metric $d_B$ on ${\Theta}$,
such that the following five properties \eqref{osccontrol}, \eqref{firstdb}, \eqref{monotonedb}, \eqref{seconddb}, and \eqref{thirddb} are satisfied.
For every ball $B \subset X$
\begin{equation} \sup_{x,y\in B}|{\vartheta}(x)-{{\vartheta}(y)}- {\theta}(x)+{{\theta}(y)}| \le d_{B}({\vartheta},{\theta})\,.
\end{equation}
For any two balls $B_1=B(x_1,R)$, $B_2= B(x_2,2R)$ in $X$ with $x_1\in B_2$ and any ${\vartheta},{\theta}\in {\Theta}$,
\begin{equation} d_{B_2}({\vartheta},{\theta})\le 2^a d_{B_1}({\vartheta},{\theta}) .
\end{equation}
For any two balls $B_1, B_2$ in $X$ with $B_1 \subset B_2$ and any ${\vartheta}, {\theta} \in {\Theta}$
\begin{equation} d_{B_1}({\vartheta},{\theta}) \le d_{B_2}({\vartheta}, {\theta})
\end{equation}
and for any two balls
$B_1=B(x_1,R)$, $B_2= B(x_2,2^aR)$
with $B_1\subset B_2$, and ${\vartheta},{\theta}\in {\Theta}$,
\begin{equation} 2d_{B_1}({\vartheta},{\theta})
\le d_{B_2}({\vartheta},{\theta}) .
\end{equation}
For every ball $B$ in $X$ and every $d_B$-ball $\tilde B$ of radius $2R$ in ${\Theta}$, there is a collection $\mathcal{B}$ of
at most $2^a$ many $d_B$-balls of radius $R$ covering $\tilde B$, that is,
\begin{equation} \tilde B\subset \bigcup \mathcal{B}.
\end{equation}
nodes.genus: collection ${\Theta}$ of real valued continuous functions
differentia: there is a point $o\in X$ where all the functions are equal to $0$
there exists for each ball $B \subset X$ a metric $d_B$ on ${\Theta}$
nodes.statement_short: $\Theta$ is compatible if all functions vanish at $o$ and ball metrics $d_B$ satisfy oscillation control, doubling and monotonicity (five properties).
nodes.section: 1.1 Statement of the metric space Carleson theorems

nodes.name: oscillation control
nodes.statement: \sup_{x,y\in B}|{\vartheta}(x)-{{\vartheta}(y)}- {\theta}(x)+{{\theta}(y)}| \le d_{B}({\vartheta},{\theta})\,.
nodes.section: 1.1 Statement of the metric space Carleson theorems
nodes.label: osccontrol

nodes.name: first doubling property of $d_B$
nodes.statement: d_{B_2}({\vartheta},{\theta})\le 2^a d_{B_1}({\vartheta},{\theta}) .
nodes.section: 1.1 Statement of the metric space Carleson theorems
nodes.label: firstdb

nodes.name: monotonicity of $d_B$
nodes.statement: d_{B_1}({\vartheta},{\theta}) \le d_{B_2}({\vartheta}, {\theta})
nodes.section: 1.1 Statement of the metric space Carleson theorems
nodes.label: monotonedb

nodes.name: second doubling property of $d_B$
nodes.statement: 2d_{B_1}({\vartheta},{\theta}) \le d_{B_2}({\vartheta},{\theta}) .
nodes.section: 1.1 Statement of the metric space Carleson theorems
nodes.label: seconddb

nodes.name: covering (third doubling) property of $d_B$
nodes.statement: \tilde B\subset \bigcup \mathcal{B}.
nodes.section: 1.1 Statement of the metric space Carleson theorems
nodes.label: thirddb

nodes.name: cancellative collection
nodes.statement:
Further, a compatible collection ${\Theta}$ is called cancellative, if
for any ball $B$ in $X$ of radius $R$, any Lipschitz function $\varphi: X\to \mathbb{C}$
supported on $B$, and any ${\vartheta},{\theta}\in {\Theta}$ we have
\begin{equation} |\int_B e({\vartheta}(x)-{{\theta}(x)}) \varphi(x) d\mu(x)|\le 2^a \mu(B)\|\varphi\|_{\operatorname{Lip}(B)}
(1+d_B({\vartheta},{\theta}))^{-\frac{1}{a}},
\end{equation}
where $\|\cdot\|_{\operatorname{Lip}(B)}$ denotes the inhomogeneous Lipschitz norm on $B$:
$$
    \|\varphi\|_{\operatorname{Lip}(B)} = \sup_{x \in B} |\varphi(x)| + R \sup_{x,y \in B, x \neq y} \frac{|\varphi(x) - \varphi(y)|}{\rho(x,y)}\,.
$$

supported on $B$, and any ${\vartheta},{\theta}\in {\Theta}$ we have

nodes.name: non-sharpness of the constant $2^{443a^3}$
nodes.statement_short: The constant $2^{443a^3}$ is not sharp; the Lean formalization gets $2^{44a^3}$ by changing $D$ to $2^{7a^3}$.
nodes.statement: The value of the constant factor $2^{443a^3}$ in Theorems~\ref{metric-space-Carleson} and~\ref{linearised-metric-Carleson} is by no means sharp. One source of non-sharpness is our choice to write for readability most constants in the form $2^{na^3}$ for some explicit constant $n$. An a posteriori byproduct of the Lean formalization of this document is that Theorems~\ref{metric-space-Carleson} and~\ref{linearised-metric-Carleson} remain true with $2^{44a^3}$ instead of $2^{443a^3}$. This is obtained by changing the parameter $D$ introduced in~\eqref{defineD} from $2^{100a^3}$ to $2^{7a^3}$, checking that exactly the same proof goes through, tracking the constants, and getting $2^{44a^3}$ in the end. This value is again by no means sharp. In the formalization we define the parameter $D$ as $2^{\mathbbm{c}a^3}$ and the constants in this blueprint are obtained by setting $\mathbbm{c} = 100$.

nodes.name: grid structure
nodes.statement:
A grid structure $(\mathcal{D}, c, s)$ on $X$ consists of a finite collection $\mathcal{D}$ of pairs $(I, k)$ of Borel
sets in $X$ and integers $k \in [-S, S]$, the projection $s\colon \mathcal{D}\to [-S, S], (I, k) \mapsto k$ to the second component which is assumed to be surjective and
called scale function, and a function $c:\mathcal{D}\to X$
called center function such that the five properties
\eqref{coverdyadic}, \eqref{dyadicproperty}, \eqref{subsetmaxcube},
\eqref{eq-vol-sp-cube}, and \eqref{eq-small-boundary} hold. We call the elements of $\mathcal{D}$ dyadic cubes. By abuse of notation, we will usually write just $I$ for the cube $(I,k)$, and we will write $I \subset J$ to mean that for two cubes $(I,k), (J, l) \in \mathcal{D}$ we have $I \subset J$ and $k \le l$.

For each dyadic cube $I$ and each $-S\le k<s(I)$ we have
\begin{equation} I\subset \bigcup_{J\in \mathcal {D}: s(J)=k}J\, .
\end{equation}
Any two non-disjoint dyadic cubes $I,J$ with $s(I)\le s(J)$ satisfy
\begin{equation} I\subset J.
\end{equation}
There exists a $I_0 \in \mathcal{D}$ with $s(I_0) = S$ and $c(I_0) = o$



and for all cubes $J \in \mathcal{D}$, we have
\begin{equation} J \subset I_0\,.
\end{equation}

For any dyadic cube $I$,
\begin{equation} c(I)\in B(c(I), \frac{1}{4} D^{s(I)}) \subset I \subset B(c(I), 4 D^{s(I)})\,.
\end{equation}
For any dyadic cube $I$ and any $t$ with $tD^{s(I)} \ge D^{-S}$,
\begin{equation} \mu(\{x \in I \ : \ \rho(x, X \setminus I) \leq t D^{s(I)}\}) \le 2 t^\kappa \mu(I)\,.
\end{equation}

sets in $X$ and integers $k \in [-S, S]$

Define for ${\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak P}$ \begin{equation} E({\mathfrak p})=\{x\in {\mathcal{I}}({\mathfrak p}): {Q}(x)\in {\Omega}({\mathfrak p}) , {\sigma_1}(x)\le {\mathrm{s}}({\mathfrak p})\le {\sigma_2}(x)\} \end{equation} and \begin{equation} T_{{\mathfrak p}} f(x)= \mathbf{1}_{E({\mathfrak p})}(x) \int K_{{\mathrm{s}}({\mathfrak p})}(x,y) f(y) e({Q}(x)(y)-{Q}(x)(x))\, d\mu(y). \end{equation} Then there exists a Borel set $G'$ with $2\mu(G') \leq \mu(G)$ such that for all Borel functions $f:X\to \mathbb{C}$ with $|f|\le \mathbf{1}_F$ we have \begin{equation} \int_{G \setminus G'} \left| \sum_{{\mathfrak p} \in {\mathfrak P}} T_{{\mathfrak p}} f (x) \right| \, \mathrm{d}\mu(x) \le \frac{2^{442a^3}}{(q-1)^5} \mu(G)^{1-\frac{1}{q}} \mu(F)^{\frac{1}{q}}\,. \end{equation}

nodes.name: $n$-forest
nodes.statement:
Let $n\ge 0$.
An $n$-forest is a pair $({\mathfrak U}, \mathfrak{T})$
where ${\mathfrak U}$ is a subset of ${\mathfrak P}$
and $\mathfrak{T}$ is a map assigning to
each ${\mathfrak u}\in {\mathfrak U}$ a nonempty set ${\mathfrak T} ({\mathfrak u})\subset {\mathfrak P}$ called tree
such that the following properties
\eqref{forest1}, \eqref{forest2},
\eqref{forest3},
\eqref{forest4},
\eqref{forest5}, and
\eqref{forest6}
hold.

For each ${\mathfrak u}\in {\mathfrak U}$ and each ${\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak T}({\mathfrak u})$
we have ${\mathcal{I}}({\mathfrak p}) \ne {\mathcal{I}}({\mathfrak u})$ and
\begin{equation} 4{\mathfrak p}\lesssim {\mathfrak u}.
\end{equation}
For each ${\mathfrak u} \in {\mathfrak U}$ and each ${\mathfrak p},{\mathfrak p}''\in {\mathfrak T}({\mathfrak u})$ and ${\mathfrak p}'\in {\mathfrak P}$
we have
\begin{equation} {\mathfrak p}, {\mathfrak p}'' \in \mathfrak{T}({\mathfrak u}), {\mathfrak p} \leq {\mathfrak p}' \leq {\mathfrak p}'' \implies {\mathfrak p}' \in \mathfrak{T}({\mathfrak u}).
\end{equation}
We have
\begin{equation} \|\sum_{{\mathfrak u}\in {\mathfrak U}} \mathbf{1}_{{\mathcal{I}}({\mathfrak u})}\|_\infty \leq 2^n\,.
\end{equation}
We have for every ${\mathfrak u}\in {\mathfrak U}$
\begin{equation} \operatorname{dens}_1({\mathfrak T}({\mathfrak u}))\le 2^{4a + 1-n}\, .
\end{equation}
We have for ${\mathfrak u}, {\mathfrak u}'\in {\mathfrak U}$ with ${\mathfrak u}\neq {\mathfrak u}'$ and ${\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak T}({\mathfrak u}')$ with ${\mathcal{I}}({\mathfrak p})\subset {\mathcal{I}}({\mathfrak u})$ that
\begin{equation} d_{{\mathfrak p}}({\mathcal{Q}}({\mathfrak p}), {\mathcal{Q}}({\mathfrak u}))>2^{Z(n+1)}\, .
\end{equation}
We have for every ${\mathfrak u}\in {\mathfrak U}$ and ${\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak T}({\mathfrak u})$ that
\begin{equation} B({\mathrm{c}}({\mathfrak p}), 8D^{{\mathrm{s}}({\mathfrak p})})\subset {\mathcal{I}}({\mathfrak u}).
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: An $n$-forest: top tiles $\mathfrak U$ with trees $\mathfrak T(\mathfrak u)$ that are convex, of overlap at most $2^n$, density $\le 2^{4a+1-n}$ and frequency-separated.
nodes.section: 2 Proof of Metric Space Carleson, overview

nodes.label: forest1

nodes.name: forest operator
assumptions: For any $n\ge 0$ and any $n$-forest $({\mathfrak U},{\mathfrak T})$
nodes.statement_short: The tile operator summed over an $n$-forest is bounded on $L^2$ by $2^{440a^3}2^{-\frac{q-1}{q}n}\mathrm{dens}_2^{1/q-1/2}$.
nodes.statement: For any $n\ge 0$ and any $n$-forest $({\mathfrak U},{\mathfrak T})$ we have for all $f,g: X \to \mathbb{C}$ with $|f| \le \mathbf{1}_F$ and $|g| \le \mathbf{1}_G$ $$ | \int \overline{g(x)} \sum_{{\mathfrak u}\in {\mathfrak U}} \sum_{{\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak T}({\mathfrak u})} T_{{\mathfrak p}} f(x) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(x)| $$ $$ \le 2^{440a^3}2^{-\frac{q-1}{q} n} \operatorname{dens}_2\left(\bigcup_{{\mathfrak u}\in {\mathfrak U}}{\mathfrak T}({\mathfrak u})\right)^{\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{2}} \|f\|_2 \|g\|_2 \,. $$

Then \begin{equation} |\int e({\vartheta}(x)-{{\theta}(x)})\varphi(x) dx|\le 2^{7a} \mu(B) \|{\varphi}\|_{C^\tau(B(z, 2R))} (1 + d_{B}({\vartheta},{\theta}))^{-\frac{1}{2a^2+a^3}} \,. \end{equation}

If for some $\lambda>0$ and some measurable function $u:X\to [0,\infty)$ we have

conclusions: there exists a measurable function $Mw: X \to [0, \infty)$ such that the following \eqref{eq-ball-av} and \eqref{eq-hlm-2} hold.

nodes.statement_short: Vitali covering bound for finite ball collections, $L^{p_2}$ bounds for $M_{\mathcal B,p_1}$, and a global maximal function $Mw$ with $L^p$ bounds.
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a finite collection of balls in $X$. If for some $\lambda>0$ and some measurable function $u:X\to [0,\infty)$ we have \begin{equation} \int_{B} u(x)\, d\mu(x)\ge \lambda \mu(B) \end{equation} for each $B\in \mathcal{B}$, then \begin{equation} \lambda \mu(\bigcup \mathcal{B}) \le 2^{2a}\int_X u(x)\, d\mu(x)\, . \end{equation} For every measurable function $v$ and $1\le p_1<p_2$ we have \begin{equation} \|M_{\mathcal{B},p_1} v\|_{p_2}\le 2^{2a}\frac{p_2}{p_2-p_1} \|v\|_{p_2}\, . \end{equation} Moreover, given any measurable bounded function $w: X \to \mathbb{C}$ there exists a measurable function $Mw: X \to [0, \infty)$ such that the following \eqref{eq-ball-av} and \eqref{eq-hlm-2} hold. For each ball $B \subset X$ and each $x \in B$ \begin{equation} \frac{1}{\mu(B)} \int_{B} |w(y)| \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) \le Mw(x) \end{equation} and for all $1 \le p_1 < p_2 \le \infty$ \begin{equation} \|M(w^{p_1})^{\frac{1}{p_1}}\|_{p_2} \le 2^{4a} \frac{p_2}{p_2-p_1}\|w\|_{p_2}\,. \end{equation}

nodes.name: ball metric entropy
assumptions: Suppose that $\mathcal{Z} \subset B_{B'}({\vartheta}, r2^k)$ satisfies that $\{B_{B'}(z,r)\mid z \in \mathcal{Z}\}$ is a collection of pairwise disjoint sets.
nodes.statement_short: A $d_{B'}$-ball of radius $r2^k$ contains at most $2^{ka}$ points with disjoint $r$-balls.
nodes.statement: Let $B' \subset X$ be a ball. Let $r > 0$, ${\vartheta} \in {\Theta}$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Suppose that $\mathcal{Z} \subset B_{B'}({\vartheta}, r2^k)$ satisfies that $\{B_{B'}(z,r)\mid z \in \mathcal{Z}\}$ is a collection of pairwise disjoint sets. Then $$ |\mathcal{Z}| \le 2^{ka}\,. $$
nodes.label: ball-metric-entropy

nodes.name: proof of ball metric entropy
nodes.statement_short: Iterate the covering property (thirddb) $k$ times; each covering ball holds at most one separated point.
nodes.statement: By applying property \eqref{thirddb} $k$ times, we obtain a collection $\mathcal{Z}' \subset {\Theta}$ with $|\mathcal{Z}'| = 2^{ka}$ and $$ B_{B'}({\vartheta},r2^k) \subset \bigcup_{z' \in \mathcal{Z}'} B_{B'}(z', \frac{r}{2})\,. $$ Then each $z \in \mathcal{Z}$ is contained in one of the balls $B(z', \frac{r}{2})$, but by the separation assumption no such ball contains more than one element of $\mathcal{Z}$. Thus $|\mathcal{Z}| \le |\mathcal{Z}'| = 2^{ka}$.

nodes.name: Cover the big ball by $2^{ka}$ balls of radius $r/2$ via (thirddb) $k$ times
nodes.statement:
By applying property \eqref{thirddb} $k$ times, we obtain a collection $\mathcal{Z}' \subset {\Theta}$ with $|\mathcal{Z}'| = 2^{ka}$ and
    $$
        B_{B'}({\vartheta},r2^k) \subset \bigcup_{z' \in \mathcal{Z}'} B_{B'}(z', \frac{r}{2})\,.
    $$
nodes.statement_short: Cover the big ball by $2^{ka}$ balls of radius $r/2$ via (thirddb) $k$ times

nodes.name: Each small ball contains at most one point of $\mathcal Z$
nodes.statement: Then each $z \in \mathcal{Z}$ is contained in one of the balls $B(z', \frac{r}{2})$, but by the separation assumption no such ball contains more than one element of $\mathcal{Z}$.
nodes.statement_short: Each small ball contains at most one point of $\mathcal Z$

nodes.name: Conclude $|\mathcal Z|\le 2^{ka}$
nodes.statement: Thus $|\mathcal{Z}| \le |\mathcal{Z}'| = 2^{ka}$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $|\mathcal Z|\le 2^{ka}$

nodes.name: monotone cube metrics
assumptions: Let $(\mathcal{D}, c, s)$ be a grid structure.
nodes.statement_short: The metrics $d_{I^\circ}$ increase with the cube, by a factor $2^{95a}$ for a strictly larger cube.
nodes.statement: Let $(\mathcal{D}, c, s)$ be a grid structure. Denote for cubes $I \in \mathcal{D}$ $$ I^\circ := B(c(I), \frac{1}{4} D^{s(I)})\,. $$ Let $I, J \in \mathcal{D}$ with $I \subset J$. Then for all ${\vartheta}, {\theta} \in{\Theta}$ we have $$ d_{I^\circ}({\vartheta}, {\theta}) \le d_{J^\circ}({\vartheta}, {\theta})\,, $$ and if $I \ne J$ then we have $$ d_{I^\circ}({\vartheta}, {\theta}) \le 2^{-95a} d_{J^\circ}({\vartheta}, {\theta})\,. $$
nodes.label: monotone-cube-metrics

nodes.name: proof of monotone cube metrics
nodes.statement_short: Equal scales force $I=J$; otherwise chain monotonicity, doubling (seconddb, firstdb) and ball inclusions.
nodes.statement: If $s(I) \ge s(J)$ then \eqref{dyadicproperty} and the assumption $I\subset J$ imply $I = J$. Then the lemma holds by reflexivity. If $s(J) \ge s(I)+1$, then using the monotonicity property \eqref{monotonedb}, \eqref{defineD} and \eqref{seconddb}, we get \begin{equation} d_{I^\circ}({\vartheta}, {\theta}) \le d_{B(c(I), 4 D^{s(I)})}({\vartheta}, {\theta}) \le 2^{-100a} d_{B(c(I), 4D^{s(J)})}({\vartheta}, {\theta})\,. \end{equation} Using \eqref{eq-vol-sp-cube}, together with the inclusion $I \subset J$, we obtain $$ c(I) \in I \subset J \subset B(c(J), 4 D^{s(J)}) $$ and consequently by the triangle inequality $$ B(c(I), 4 D^{s(J)}) \subset B(c(J), 8 D^{s(J)})\,. $$ Using this together with the monotonicity property \eqref{monotonedb} and \eqref{firstdb} in \eqref{eq-dIJ-est}, we obtain \begin{align*} d_{I^\circ}({\vartheta}, {\theta}) &\le 2^{-100a} d_{B(c(J), 8D^{s(J)})}({\vartheta}, {\theta})\\ &\le 2^{-100a + 5a} d_{B(c(J), \frac{1}{4}D^{s(J)})}({\vartheta}, {\theta})\\ &= 2^{-95a}d_{J^\circ}({\vartheta}, {\theta})\,. \end{align*} This proves the second inequality claimed in the Lemma, from which the first follows since $a \ge 4$ and hence $2^{-95a} \le 1$.

nodes.name: Case $s(I)\ge s(J)$: then $I=J$
nodes.statement: If $s(I) \ge s(J)$ then \eqref{dyadicproperty} and the assumption $I\subset J$ imply $I = J$. Then the lemma holds by reflexivity.
nodes.statement_short: Case $s(I)\ge s(J)$: then $I=J$

nodes.name: Case $s(J)\ge s(I)+1$: gain $2^{-95a}$
nodes.statement:
If $s(J) \ge s(I)+1$, then using the monotonicity property \eqref{monotonedb}, \eqref{defineD} and \eqref{seconddb}, we get
    \begin{equation} d_{I^\circ}({\vartheta}, {\theta}) \le d_{B(c(I), 4 D^{s(I)})}({\vartheta}, {\theta}) \le 2^{-100a} d_{B(c(I), 4D^{s(J)})}({\vartheta}, {\theta})\,.
    \end{equation}
    Using \eqref{eq-vol-sp-cube}, together with the inclusion $I \subset J$, we obtain
    $$
        c(I) \in I \subset J \subset B(c(J), 4 D^{s(J)})
    $$
    and consequently by the triangle inequality
    $$
        B(c(I), 4 D^{s(J)}) \subset B(c(J), 8 D^{s(J)})\,.
    $$
    Using this together with the monotonicity property \eqref{monotonedb} and \eqref{firstdb} in \eqref{eq-dIJ-est}, we obtain

        &\le 2^{-100a + 5a} d_{B(c(J), \frac{1}{4}D^{s(J)})}({\vartheta}, {\theta})\\
        &= 2^{-95a}d_{J^\circ}({\vartheta}, {\theta})\,.
    \end{align*}
    This proves the second inequality claimed in the Lemma, from which the first follows since $a \ge 4$ and hence $2^{-95a} \le 1$.

nodes.name: kernel summand
nodes.statement_short: Support, size and Hölder-smoothness bounds for the truncated kernels $K_s$.
nodes.statement: Let $-S\le s\le S$ and $x,y,y'\in X$. If $K_s(x,y)\neq 0$, then we have \begin{equation} \frac{1}{4} D^{s-1} \leq \rho(x,y) \leq \frac{1}{2} D^s\, . \end{equation} We have \begin{equation} |K_s(x,y)|\le \frac{2^{102 a^3}}{\mu(B(x, D^{s}))}\, \end{equation} and \begin{equation} |K_s(x,y)-K_s(x, y')|\le \frac{2^{127a^3}}{\mu(B(x, D^{s}))} \left(\frac{ \rho(y,y')}{D^s}\right)^{\frac 1a}\,. \end{equation}
nodes.label: kernel-summand

nodes.name: support of $K_s$

nodes.label: supp-Ks

nodes.statement: |K_s(x,y)-K_s(x, y')|\le \frac{2^{127a^3}}{\mu(B(x, D^{s}))} \left(\frac{ \rho(y,y')}{D^s}\right)^{\frac 1a}\,.

nodes.name: proof of kernel summand
nodes.statement_short: Support from the definition of $\psi$; size via kernel bound and doubling; smoothness split by whether $2\rho(y,y')\le\rho(x,y)$, using kernel smoothness and the $4D$-Lipschitz bound of $\psi$.
nodes.statement: By Definition \eqref{defks}, the function $K_s$ is the product of $K$ with a function which is supported in the set of all $x,y$ satisfying \eqref{supp-Ks}. This proves \eqref{supp-Ks}. Using \eqref{eqkernel-size} and the lower bound in \eqref{supp-Ks} we obtain \begin{equation} |K_s(x,y)|\le |K(x,y)|\le \frac{2^{a^3}}{\mu(B(x,\frac 14 D^{s-1}))} \end{equation} Using $D=2^{100a^2}$ and the doubling property \eqref{doublingx} $2 +100a^2$ times estimates the last display by \begin{equation} \le \frac{2^{2a+101a^3}}{\mu(B(x, D^{s}))}\, . \end{equation} Using $a\ge 4$ proves \eqref{eq-Ks-size}. To prove \eqref{eq-Ks-smooth} when $2\rho(y,y') > \rho(x,y)$, use the lower bound in \eqref{supp-Ks} and the inequality $2\rho(y,y') > \frac{1}{4}D^{s-1}$. Then \eqref{eq-Ks-smooth} follows from the triangle inequality, \eqref{eq-Ks-size} and $a \ge 4$. If $2\rho(y,y') \le \rho(x,y)$, we rewrite $|K_s(x,y)-K_s(x, y')|$ as \begin{equation} |(K(x,y)-K(x,y')) \psi(D^{-s}\rho(x,y)) + K(x,y)(\psi(D^{-s}\rho(x,y))-\psi(D^{-s}\rho(x,y')))|\,. \end{equation} An upper bound for $|K(x,y)-K(x, y')|$ is obtained similarly to the proof of \eqref{eq-Ks-size}, using \eqref{eqkernel-y-smooth} and the lower bound in \eqref{supp-Ks} \begin{equation} |K(x,y)-K(x, y')|\le \frac{2^{a^3}}{\mu(B(x, \frac 14 D^{s-1}))} \left(\frac{ \rho(y,y')}{\frac 14 D^{s-1}}\right)^{\frac 1a}\,. \end{equation} As above, this is estimated by \begin{equation} \le \frac{4D 2^{2a+101a^3}}{\mu(B(x, D^{s}))} \left(\frac{ \rho(y,y')}{D^{s}}\right)^{\frac 1a} = \frac{2^{2+2a+100a^2+101a^3}}{\mu(B(x, D^{s}))} \left(\frac{ \rho(y,y')}{D^{s}}\right)^{\frac 1a}\,. \end{equation} We have the trivial bound $|\psi(D^{-s}\rho(x,y))| \leq 1$, and \eqref{eq-Ks-aux} provides a bound for $|K(x,y)|$. Finally, we show that \begin{equation} |\psi(D^{-s}\rho(x,y))-\psi(D^{-s}\rho(x,y'))|\le 4D \left(\frac{\rho(y, y')}{D ^ s}\right)^{\frac 1a} \end{equation} by considering separately the cases $\rho(y,y')/D^s \ge 1$ and $\rho(y,y')/D^s < 1$. In the former case, the inequality is trivial; in the latter case, it follows from the fact that $\psi$ is Lipschitz with constant $4D$. Combining the above bounds and using $a\ge 4$ proves \eqref{eq-Ks-smooth} when $2\rho(y,y') \le \rho(x,y)$.

nodes.name: Continuity of the truncated integrand (int continuous)
nodes.statement_short: The truncated oscillatory integral $G(x,\vartheta,R_1,R_2)$ is continuous in $\vartheta$, one-sided continuous in the radii, and measurable and bounded in $x$.
conclusions: is continuous in ${\vartheta}$ for fixed $x, R_1, R_2$
It is right-continuous in $R_1$ for fixed $x, \vartheta, R_2$ and left-continuous in $R_2$ for fixed $x, \vartheta, R_1$
it is measurable in $x$ and bounded for fixed $\vartheta, R_1, R_2$
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a measurable function with $|f| \le 1$. Then the function \[ G: X \times \Theta \times (0,\infty) \times (0, \infty) \to \mathbb{C} \] \[ G(x, {\vartheta}, R_1, R_2) := \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K(x,y) f(y) e({\vartheta}(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) \] is continuous in ${\vartheta}$ for fixed $x, R_1, R_2$. It is right-continuous in $R_1$ for fixed $x, \vartheta, R_2$ and left-continuous in $R_2$ for fixed $x, \vartheta, R_1$. Finally, it is measurable in $x$ and bounded for fixed $\vartheta, R_1, R_2$.
nodes.label: int-continuous

nodes.name: Proof of the int continuous lemma
nodes.statement_short: Fubini for measurability, monotone convergence for continuity in the radii, and a Lipschitz bound via the kernel size and the doubling property for continuity in $\vartheta$.
nodes.statement: Measurability in $x$ follows from joint measurability of \[ K(x,y) \mathbf{1}_{B(x,R_2) \setminus B(x,R_1)}(y) \] in $x$ and $y$ and (part of the proof of) Fubini's theorem. (Partial) continuity in $R_1$ and $R_2$ is also a standard lemma in measure theory. It follows for example by splitting the integrand as $F_1 - F_{-1} + iF_i - iF_{-i}$ for positive, disjointly supported functions $F_{-}$ and applying the monotone convergence theorem to each summand. For continuity in ${\vartheta}$ note that \[ |G(x, {\vartheta}, R_1, R_2) - G(x, {\vartheta}', R_1, R_2)| \] \[ = \left| \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K(x,y) f(y) (e({\vartheta}(y)) - e({\vartheta}'(y))) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) \right| \] \[ \le \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} |K(x,y)| |f(y)| |e({\vartheta}(y) - {\vartheta}'(y) - {\vartheta}(o) + {\vartheta}'(o)) - 1| \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y). \] By $1$-Lipschitz continuity of $e^{ix}$, the property \eqref{osccontrol} of the metrics $d$, the kernel upper bound \eqref{eqkernel-size} and $|f| \le 1$ this is \[ \le \mu(B(x, R_2)) \sup_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} \frac{2^{a^3}}{V(x,y)} d_{B(x,\rho(o,x)+R_2)}(\vartheta, \vartheta'). \] If $R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2$ then there exists $n$ with $B(x,R_2) \subset B(x, 2^n \rho(x,y))$ and $2^n \le 2 R_2/R_1$. Hence, by the doubling property \eqref{doublingx}, \[ V(x,y) = \mu(B(x, \rho(x,y))) \ge 2^{-an} \mu(B(x, R_2)) \ge (2R_2 / R_1)^{-a} \mu(B(x, R_2)). \] Hence \[ |G(x, {\vartheta}, R_1, R_2) - G(x, {\vartheta}', R_1, R_2)| \le 2^{a^3} \Big(\frac{2R_2}{R_1}\Big)^a d_{B(x, \rho(o,x)+R_2)}({\vartheta}, {\vartheta}'). \] Since the topology on ${\Theta}$ is the one induced by any of the metrics $d_B$, continuity follows. Finally, for boundedness as a function of $x$ note that we also have by a similar computation using $|e({\vartheta})|=1$ \[ |G(x, {\vartheta}, R_1, R_2)| \le 2^{a^3} \Big(\frac{2R_2}{R_1}\Big)^a. \]

nodes.name: Measurability in x
nodes.statement:
Measurability in $x$ follows from joint measurability of
    \[
        K(x,y) \mathbf{1}_{B(x,R_2) \setminus B(x,R_1)}(y)
    \]
    in $x$ and $y$ and (part of the proof of) Fubini's theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Measurability in $x$ via Fubini

nodes.name: Continuity in radii
nodes.statement: (Partial) continuity in $R_1$ and $R_2$ is also a standard lemma in measure theory. It follows for example by splitting the integrand as $F_1 - F_{-1} + iF_i - iF_{-i}$ for positive, disjointly supported functions $F_{-}$ and applying the monotone convergence theorem to each summand.
nodes.statement_short: One-sided continuity in the radii via monotone convergence

nodes.name: Difference of integrands
nodes.statement:
For continuity in ${\vartheta}$ note that
    \[
        |G(x, {\vartheta}, R_1, R_2) - G(x, {\vartheta}', R_1, R_2)|
    \]
    \[
        = \left| \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K(x,y) f(y) (e({\vartheta}(y)) - e({\vartheta}'(y))) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) \right|
    \]
    \[
        \le \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} |K(x,y)| |f(y)| |e({\vartheta}(y) - {\vartheta}'(y) - {\vartheta}(o) + {\vartheta}'(o)) - 1| \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y).
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Write the difference $G(\vartheta)-G(\vartheta')$ as an integral of $|e(\cdot)-1|$

nodes.name: Lipschitz bound
nodes.statement:
By $1$-Lipschitz continuity of $e^{ix}$, the property \eqref{osccontrol} of the metrics $d$, the kernel upper bound \eqref{eqkernel-size} and $|f| \le 1$ this is
    \[
        \le \mu(B(x, R_2)) \sup_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} \frac{2^{a^3}}{V(x,y)} d_{B(x,\rho(o,x)+R_2)}(\vartheta, \vartheta').
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound by the oscillation metric using kernel size

nodes.name: Doubling lower bound
nodes.statement:
If $R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2$ then there exists $n$ with $B(x,R_2) \subset B(x, 2^n \rho(x,y))$ and $2^n \le 2 R_2/R_1$. Hence, by the doubling property \eqref{doublingx},
    \[
        V(x,y) = \mu(B(x, \rho(x,y))) \ge 2^{-an} \mu(B(x, R_2)) \ge (2R_2 / R_1)^{-a} \mu(B(x, R_2)).
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound $V(x,y)$ by doubling

nodes.name: Continuity in theta
nodes.statement:
Hence
    \[
        |G(x, {\vartheta}, R_1, R_2) - G(x, {\vartheta}', R_1, R_2)| \le 2^{a^3} \Big(\frac{2R_2}{R_1}\Big)^a d_{B(x, \rho(o,x)+R_2)}({\vartheta}, {\vartheta}').
    \]
    Since the topology on ${\Theta}$ is the one induced by any of the metrics $d_B$, continuity follows.
nodes.statement_short: Combine to a Lipschitz estimate in $d_B$, giving continuity

nodes.name: Boundedness
nodes.statement:
Finally, for boundedness as a function of $x$ note that we also have by a similar computation using $|e({\vartheta})|=1$
    \[
        |G(x, {\vartheta}, R_1, R_2)| \le 2^{a^3} \Big(\frac{2R_2}{R_1}\Big)^a.
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Boundedness by the same computation

nodes.name: Proof of Metric Space Carleson
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the supremum to a countable dense set, approximate by finite sets with measurable maximizers $Q_n$, and apply the linearised theorem via monotone convergence.
nodes.statement: Let Borel sets $F$, $G$ in $X$ be given. Let a Borel function $f: X \to \mathbb{C}$ with $f \le \mathbf{1}_F$ be given. Let ${\Theta}' \subset {\Theta}$ be a countable dense set. By Lemma \ref{int-continuous} we have \[ \sup_{{\vartheta}\in{\Theta}} \sup_{0 < R_1 < R_2}\left| \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K(x,y) f(y) e({\vartheta}(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) \right| \] \[ = \sup_{{\vartheta}\in{\Theta}'} \sup_{0 < R_1 < R_2, R_i \in \mathbb{Q}}\left| \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K(x,y) f(y) e({\vartheta}(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) \right|. \] Consider an enumeration of ${\Theta}'$ and let ${\Theta}_n$ be the finite set consisting of the first $n+1$ functions in the enumeration. Then by the monotone convergence theorem \[ \Big| \int_G Tf \, \mathrm{d}\mu\Big| \] \[ = \int_G \sup_{{\vartheta}\in{\Theta}'} \sup_{0 < R_1 < R_2, R_i \in \mathbb{Q}}\left| \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K(x,y) f(y) e({\vartheta}(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) \right| \, \mathrm{d}\mu(x) \] \[ = \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_G \sup_{{\vartheta}\in{\Theta}_n} \sup_{0 < R_1 < R_2, R_i \in \mathbb{Q}}\left| \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K(x,y) f(y) e({\vartheta}(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) \right| \, \mathrm{d}\mu(x). \] For each $n$, let $Q_n(x)$ be the measurable function specifying the maximizer in the supremum in ${\vartheta}$ in the previous line. It is possible to construct such a measurable function of $x$, because the function inside the supremum is measurable in $x$, being a countable supremum of measurable functions, and because ${\Theta}_n$ is finite. (For example one may fix some order on the finite set ${\Theta}_n$ and pick the smallest maximizer with respect to that order. This is a measurable choice function.) Then the previous display becomes \[ \le \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_G \sup_{0 < R_1 < R_2} \left| \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K(x,y) f(y) e(Q_n(x)(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) \right| \, \mathrm{d}\mu(x). \] \[ = \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_G T_{Q_n} f \, \mathrm{d}\mu. \] It remains to verify the assumptions of Theorem \ref{linearised-metric-Carleson}, which when applied here completes the proof. The assumptions of Theorem \ref{metric-space-Carleson} and Theorem \ref{linearised-metric-Carleson} are the same, with the exception of the assumption \eqref{linnontanbound}. The assumption \eqref{linnontanbound} however is weaker than the assumption \eqref{nontanbound} of Theorem \ref{metric-space-Carleson}. Indeed, setting for fixed $x, {\vartheta}$ the outer radius $R_2$ in \eqref{def-tang-unm-op} to $\min\{R_2', R_Q({\vartheta}, x')\}$, where $R_2'$ is the outer radius in \eqref{def-lin-star-op}, shows that \eqref{def-lin-star-op} is smaller than or equal to \eqref{def-tang-unm-op}. Thus we can apply Theorem \ref{linearised-metric-Carleson}, which completes the proof.

nodes.name: Fix data
nodes.statement: Let Borel sets $F$, $G$ in $X$ be given. Let a Borel function $f: X \to \mathbb{C}$ with $f \le \mathbf{1}_F$ be given.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $F$, $G$, $f$

nodes.name: Countable reduction
nodes.statement:
Let ${\Theta}' \subset {\Theta}$ be a countable dense set. By Lemma \ref{int-continuous} we have
    \[
        \sup_{{\vartheta}\in{\Theta}} \sup_{0 < R_1 < R_2}\left| \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K(x,y) f(y) e({\vartheta}(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) \right|
    \]
    \[
        = \sup_{{\vartheta}\in{\Theta}'} \sup_{0 < R_1 < R_2, R_i \in \mathbb{Q}}\left| \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K(x,y) f(y) e({\vartheta}(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) \right|.
    \]
nodes.statement_short: By the continuity lemma, restrict the suprema to a countable dense set and rational radii

nodes.name: Finite approximation
nodes.statement:
Consider an enumeration of ${\Theta}'$ and let ${\Theta}_n$ be the finite set consisting of the first $n+1$ functions in the enumeration. Then by the monotone convergence theorem
    \[
        \Big| \int_G Tf \, \mathrm{d}\mu\Big|
    \]
    \[
        = \int_G \sup_{{\vartheta}\in{\Theta}'} \sup_{0 < R_1 < R_2, R_i \in \mathbb{Q}}\left| \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K(x,y) f(y) e({\vartheta}(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) \right| \, \mathrm{d}\mu(x)
    \]
    \[
        = \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_G \sup_{{\vartheta}\in{\Theta}_n} \sup_{0 < R_1 < R_2, R_i \in \mathbb{Q}}\left| \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K(x,y) f(y) e({\vartheta}(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) \right| \, \mathrm{d}\mu(x).
    \]
    For each
nodes.statement_short: Exhaust $\Theta'$ by finite sets $\Theta_n$ and use monotone convergence

nodes.name: Measurable maximizer
nodes.statement: For each $n$, let $Q_n(x)$ be the measurable function specifying the maximizer in the supremum in ${\vartheta}$ in the previous line. It is possible to construct such a measurable function of $x$, because the function inside the supremum is measurable in $x$, being a countable supremum of measurable functions, and because ${\Theta}_n$ is finite. (For example one may fix some order on the finite set ${\Theta}_n$ and pick the smallest maximizer with respect to that order. This is a measurable choice function.)
nodes.statement_short: Choose a measurable maximizer $Q_n$

nodes.name: Linearisation
nodes.statement:
Then the previous display becomes
    \[
        \le \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_G \sup_{0 < R_1 < R_2} \left| \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K(x,y) f(y) e(Q_n(x)(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) \right| \, \mathrm{d}\mu(x).
    \]
    \[
        = \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_G T_{Q_n} f \, \mathrm{d}\mu.
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound by the linearised operators $T_{Q_n}$

nodes.name: Remaining hypotheses
nodes.statement: It remains to verify the assumptions of Theorem \ref{linearised-metric-Carleson}, which when applied here completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to checking hypotheses of the linearised theorem

nodes.name: Hypothesis comparison
nodes.statement:
The assumptions of Theorem \ref{metric-space-Carleson} and Theorem \ref{linearised-metric-Carleson} are the same,
    with the exception of the assumption \eqref{linnontanbound}.
    The assumption \eqref{linnontanbound} however is weaker than the assumption \eqref{nontanbound}
    of Theorem \ref{metric-space-Carleson}.
    Indeed, setting for fixed $x, {\vartheta}$ the outer radius $R_2$ in \eqref{def-tang-unm-op} to
    $\min\{R_2', R_Q({\vartheta}, x')\}$, where $R_2'$ is the outer radius in \eqref{def-lin-star-op},
    shows that \eqref{def-lin-star-op} is smaller than or equal to \eqref{def-tang-unm-op}.
nodes.statement_short: The linearised hypothesis is weaker than the nontangential one

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Thus we can apply Theorem \ref{linearised-metric-Carleson}, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the linearised theorem

nodes.name: Proof of the linearised metric space Carleson theorem
nodes.statement_short: Write $T_Q f$ as an increasing limit of truncations $T_{R_1,R_2,2^n}$ and apply monotone convergence with the R truncation lemma.
nodes.statement: Let Borel sets $F$, $G$ in $X$ with finite measure be given. Let a Borel function $f: X \to \mathbb{C}$ with $f \le \mathbf{1}_F$ be given. For each $0 < R_1,R_2,R$, we define $T_{R_1,R_2,R}f$ as in \eqref{TRR}. By Lemma \ref{int-continuous}, $T_{R_1,R_2,R}f$ is measurable and bounded, and we clearly have for each $x \in X$ \[ T_Q f(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sup_{2^{-n} < R_1 < R_2 < 2^n} T_{R_1, R_2, 2^n}f(x). \] For each $x$ and all $f$, the functions $\sup_{2^{-n} < R_1 < R_2 < 2^n} T_{R_1, R_2, 2^n} f(x)$ are measurable by Lemma \ref{int-continuous} and form an increasing sequence in $n$. By the monotone convergence theorem, the claimed estimate \eqref{linresweak} then follows from Lemma \ref{R-truncation}.

nodes.name: Fix data
nodes.statement: Let Borel sets $F$, $G$ in $X$ with finite measure be given. Let a Borel function $f: X \to \mathbb{C}$ with $f \le \mathbf{1}_F$ be given.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $F$, $G$, $f$

nodes.name: Truncation
nodes.statement:
For each $0 < R_1,R_2,R$, we define $T_{R_1,R_2,R}f$ as in \eqref{TRR}.
By Lemma \ref{int-continuous},
$T_{R_1,R_2,R}f$
is measurable and bounded, and we clearly have for each $x \in X$
\[
    T_Q f(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sup_{2^{-n} < R_1 < R_2 < 2^n} T_{R_1, R_2, 2^n}f(x).
\]
nodes.statement_short: Truncated operators are measurable and bounded and approximate $T_Q f$

nodes.name: Monotonicity
nodes.statement: For each $x$ and all $f$, the functions $\sup_{2^{-n} < R_1 < R_2 < 2^n} T_{R_1, R_2, 2^n} f(x)$ are measurable by Lemma \ref{int-continuous} and form an increasing sequence in $n$.
nodes.statement_short: The truncated suprema increase in $n$

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: By the monotone convergence theorem, the claimed estimate \eqref{linresweak} then follows from Lemma \ref{R-truncation}.
nodes.statement_short: Monotone convergence plus the R truncation lemma

nodes.name: R truncation
nodes.statement_short: Weak-type bound for the truncated linearised operator $T_{R_1,R_2,R}$, uniformly in the truncation radii.
nodes.statement: Let $F$, $G$ be Borel sets in $X$. Let $f:X\to \mathbb{C}$ be a Borel function with $|f|\le 1_F$. Then for all $R\in 2^{\mathbb{N}}$ we have \begin{equation} \int \mathbf{1}_G \sup_{1/R<R_1<R_2<R} |T_{R_1,R_2,R} f(x)|\, d\mu(x) \le \frac{2^{443a^3}}{(q-1)^6} \mu(G)^{1-\frac{1}{q}} \mu(F)^{\frac{1}{q}}, \end{equation} where \begin{equation} T_{R_1,R_2,R} f(x)= \mathbf{1}_{B(o,R)}(x) \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K(x,y) f(y) e(Q(x)(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) . \end{equation}
nodes.label: R-truncation

nodes.name: Truncated linearised operator $T_{R_1,R_2,R}$
nodes.statement: T_{R_1,R_2,R} f(x)= \mathbf{1}_{B(o,R)}(x) \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K(x,y) f(y) e(Q(x)(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) .
nodes.label: TRR

nodes.name: Proof of the R truncation lemma
nodes.statement_short: Decompose the kernel into the pieces $K_s$, bound the middle scales by the S truncation lemma and the boundary scales by the Hardy-Littlewood maximal function.
nodes.statement: Let $F,G,f$ as in the lemma be given. Let $R\in 2^{\mathbb{N}}$ be given. By replacing $G$ with $G\cap B(o,R)$ if necessary, a replacement that does not change the conclusion of the Lemma \ref{R-truncation}, it suffices to show \eqref{Rcut} under the assumption that $G$ is contained in $B(o,R)$ and thus bounded. We make this assumption. For every $x\in G$ and $R_2 < R$, the domain of integration in \eqref{TRR} is contained in $B(o,2R)$. By replacing $F$ with $F\cap B(o,2R)$ if necessary, and correspondingly restricting $f$ to $B(o, 2R)$, it suffices to show \eqref{Rcut} under the assumption that $F$ is contained in $B(o,2R)$ and thus bounded. We make this assumption. Using the definition \eqref{defks} of $K_s$ and the partition of unity \eqref{eq-psisum}, we observe that for fixed $R_1<R_2$ we have \begin{equation} K(x,y)\mathbf{1}_{R_1<\rho(x,y)<R_2}=\sum_{s=s_1-2}^{s_2+2} K_s(x,y) \mathbf{1}_{R_1<\rho(x,y)<R_2}, \end{equation} where $s_1=\lfloor\log_D 2R_1\rfloor+3$ and $s_2=\lceil\log_D 4R_2\rceil-2$. To obtain the identity \eqref{KKs}, we have used that on the set where $R_1<\rho(x,y)<R_2$ the kernels $K_s$ vanish unless $s$ is inside the interval of summation in \eqref{KKs}. Similarly, we observe \begin{equation} \sum_{s=s_1}^{s_2} K_s(x,y) \mathbf{1}_{R_1<\rho(x,y)<R_2} = \sum_{s=s_1}^{s_2} K_s(x,y), \end{equation} because on the support of $K_s$ with $s_1\le s\le s_2$ we have necessarily $R_1<\rho(x,y)<R_2$. We thus express \eqref{TRR} as the sum of \begin{equation} T_{s_1,s_2}f(x):=\sum_{s_1 \le s\le s_2} \int K_s(x,y) f(y) e(Q(x)(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \sum_{s=s_1-2,s_1-1, s_2+1, s_2+2} \int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K_s(x,y) f(y) e(Q(x)(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y), \end{equation} We apply the triangle inequality and estimate \eqref{Rcut} separately with $T_{R_1,R_2,R}$ replaced by \eqref{middles} and by \eqref{boundarys}. To handle the case \eqref{middles}, we employ \Cref{S-truncation}. Here, we utilize the fact that if $\frac 1R\le R_1\le R_2\le R$, then $s_1$ and $s_2$ as in \eqref{middles} are in an interval $[-S,S]$ for some sufficiently large $S$ depending on $R$. To handle the case \eqref{boundarys}, we use the triangle inequality and the properties \eqref{supp-Ks}, \eqref{eq-Ks-size} of $K_s$ and $|f| \le \mathbf{1}_F$ to obtain for arbitrary $s$ the inequality \begin{multline} \left|\int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K_s(x,y) f(y) e(Q(x)(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y)\right|\\ \leq \frac{2^{102 a^3}}{\mu(B(x, D^{s}))} \int_{B(x, D^s)} \mathbf{1}_F(y) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) \leq 2^{102 a^3} M\mathbf{1}_F(x), \end{multline} where $M\mathbf{1}_F$ is as defined in \Cref{Hardy-Littlewood}. Now the left-hand side of \eqref{Rcut}, with $T_{R_1,R_2,R}$ replaced by \eqref{boundarys}, can be estimated using H\"older's inequality and \Cref{Hardy-Littlewood} by $$ 2^{102a^3+2}\int \mathbf{1}_{G}(x) M\mathbf{1}_F(x)\, d\mu(x) \le \frac{2^{102a^3+4a+3}q}{q-1}\mu(G)^{1-\frac{1}{q}} \mu(F)^{\frac{1}{q}}\,. $$ Summing the contributions from \eqref{middles} and \eqref{boundarys} completes the proof.

nodes.name: Fix data
nodes.statement: Let $F,G,f$ as in the lemma be given. Let $R\in 2^{\mathbb{N}}$ be given.
nodes.statement_short: Fix data and $R$

nodes.name: Restrict G
nodes.statement: By replacing $G$ with $G\cap B(o,R)$ if necessary, a replacement that does not change the conclusion of the Lemma \ref{R-truncation}, it suffices to show \eqref{Rcut} under the assumption that $G$ is contained in $B(o,R)$ and thus bounded. We make this assumption.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $G\subset B(o,R)$

nodes.name: Restrict F
nodes.statement: For every $x\in G$ and $R_2 < R$, the domain of integration in \eqref{TRR} is contained in $B(o,2R)$. By replacing $F$ with $F\cap B(o,2R)$ if necessary, and correspondingly restricting $f$ to $B(o, 2R)$, it suffices to show \eqref{Rcut} under the assumption that $F$ is contained in $B(o,2R)$ and thus bounded. We make this assumption.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $F\subset B(o,2R)$

nodes.name: Kernel decomposition
nodes.statement:
Using the definition \eqref{defks} of $K_s$ and the partition of unity \eqref{eq-psisum},
we observe that
for fixed $R_1<R_2$ we have
\begin{equation} K(x,y)\mathbf{1}_{R_1<\rho(x,y)<R_2}=\sum_{s=s_1-2}^{s_2+2} K_s(x,y) \mathbf{1}_{R_1<\rho(x,y)<R_2},
\end{equation}
where $s_1=\lfloor\log_D 2R_1\rfloor+3$ and $s_2=\lceil\log_D 4R_2\rceil-2$.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose the truncated kernel into the $K_s$

nodes.name: Support justification
nodes.statement: To obtain the identity \eqref{KKs}, we have used that on the set where $R_1<\rho(x,y)<R_2$ the kernels $K_s$ vanish unless $s$ is inside the interval of summation in \eqref{KKs}.
nodes.statement_short: Justify the summation range via the support of $K_s$

nodes.name: Middle-scale identity
nodes.statement:
Similarly, we observe
\begin{equation} \sum_{s=s_1}^{s_2} K_s(x,y) \mathbf{1}_{R_1<\rho(x,y)<R_2} = \sum_{s=s_1}^{s_2} K_s(x,y),
\end{equation}
because on the support of $K_s$ with $s_1\le s\le s_2$ we have necessarily $R_1<\rho(x,y)<R_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Middle scales need no truncation

nodes.name: Split
nodes.statement_short: Split $T_{R_1,R_2,R}$ into middle and boundary scales

nodes.name: Operator $T_{s_1,s_2}$
nodes.statement: T_{s_1,s_2}f(x):=\sum_{s_1 \le s\le s_2} \int K_s(x,y) f(y) e(Q(x)(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y)
nodes.label: middles

nodes.name: Separate estimates
nodes.statement: We apply the triangle inequality and estimate \eqref{Rcut} separately with $T_{R_1,R_2,R}$ replaced by \eqref{middles} and by \eqref{boundarys}.
nodes.statement_short: Estimate the two parts separately

nodes.name: Middle scales
nodes.statement: To handle the case \eqref{middles}, we employ \Cref{S-truncation}. Here, we utilize the fact that if $\frac 1R\le R_1\le R_2\le R$, then $s_1$ and $s_2$ as in \eqref{middles} are in an interval $[-S,S]$ for some sufficiently large $S$ depending on $R$.
nodes.statement_short: Middle scales by the S truncation lemma

nodes.name: Boundary scales
nodes.statement_short: Boundary scales are dominated by the maximal function of $\mathbf{1}_F$

nodes.name: Boundary-scale maximal function bound
nodes.statement: \left|\int_{R_1 < \rho(x,y) < R_2} K_s(x,y) f(y) e(Q(x)(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y)\right|\\ \leq \frac{2^{102 a^3}}{\mu(B(x, D^{s}))} \int_{B(x, D^s)} \mathbf{1}_F(y) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y) \leq 2^{102 a^3} M\mathbf{1}_F(x),

nodes.name: Maximal function bound
nodes.statement:
Now the left-hand side of \eqref{Rcut}, with $T_{R_1,R_2,R}$ replaced by \eqref{boundarys}, can be estimated using H\"older's inequality and \Cref{Hardy-Littlewood} by
$$
    2^{102a^3+2}\int \mathbf{1}_{G}(x) M\mathbf{1}_F(x)\, d\mu(x)
    \le \frac{2^{102a^3+4a+3}q}{q-1}\mu(G)^{1-\frac{1}{q}} \mu(F)^{\frac{1}{q}}\,.
$$
nodes.statement_short: Hölder and the Hardy-Littlewood bound

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Summing the contributions from \eqref{middles} and \eqref{boundarys} completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Sum the two estimates

nodes.name: S truncation
nodes.statement_short: Weak-type bound for the maximal truncation over scale ranges $[s_1,s_2]\subset[-S,S]$ of the linearised operator.
nodes.statement: Let $F$, $G$ be bounded Borel sets in $X$. Let $f:X\to \mathbb{C}$ be a Borel function with $|f|\le 1_F$. Then for all $S\in{\mathbb{Z}}$ we have \begin{equation} \int \mathbf{1}_G(x) \sup_{-S\le s_1\le s_2\le S} |T_{s_1,s_2} f(x)|\, d\mu(x) \le \frac{2^{442a^3+2}}{(q-1)^6} \mu(G)^{1-\frac{1}{q}} \mu(F)^{\frac{1}{q}}, \end{equation} where \begin{equation} T_{s_1,s_2} f(x) = \sum_{s_1\le s \le s_2} \int_X K_s(x,y) f(y) e(Q(x)(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y). \end{equation}
nodes.label: S-truncation

nodes.name: Operator $T_{s_1,s_2}$ (Tss)
nodes.statement: T_{s_1,s_2} f(x) = \sum_{s_1\le s \le s_2} \int_X K_s(x,y) f(y) e(Q(x)(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y).
nodes.label: Tss

nodes.name: Proof of the S truncation lemma
nodes.statement_short: Linearise the supremum over $s_1\le s_2$ by choosing measurable minimal maximizers $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$, then apply the linearized truncation lemma.
nodes.statement: We reduce \Cref{S-truncation} to \Cref{linearized-truncation}. For each $x$, let $\sigma_1(x)$ be the minimal element $s'\in [-S,S]$ such that \[ \max_{s'\le s_2\le S} |T_{s',s_2} f(x)| = \max_{-S\le s_1\le s_2\le S} |T_{s_1,s_2} f(x)| =: T_{1,x}. \] Similarly, let ${\sigma}_2(x)$ be the minimal element $s''\in [-S,S]$ such that \[ |T_{\sigma_2(x), s''} f(x)| = T_{1,x}\,. \] With these choices, and noting that with the definition of $T_{2, \sigma_1, \sigma_2}$ from \eqref{middles1} \begin{equation*} T_{\sigma_1(x),\sigma_2(x)} f(x)=T_{2,\sigma_1,\sigma_2} f(x), \end{equation*} we conclude that the left-hand side of \eqref{Scut} and \eqref{Sqlin} are equal. Therefore, \Cref{S-truncation} follows from \Cref{linearized-truncation}.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: We reduce \Cref{S-truncation} to \Cref{linearized-truncation}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the linearized truncation lemma

nodes.name: Choose sigma
nodes.statement:
For each $x$, let $\sigma_1(x)$ be the
    minimal element $s'\in [-S,S]$ such that
    \[
    \max_{s'\le s_2\le S} |T_{s',s_2} f(x)| = \max_{-S\le s_1\le s_2\le S} |T_{s_1,s_2} f(x)| =: T_{1,x}.
    \]
    Similarly, let ${\sigma}_2(x)$ be the minimal element $s''\in [-S,S]$ such that
    \[
    |T_{\sigma_2(x), s''} f(x)| = T_{1,x}\,.
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ as minimal maximizers

nodes.name: Identify LHS
nodes.statement_short: The two left-hand sides coincide

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Therefore, \Cref{S-truncation} follows from \Cref{linearized-truncation}.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by the linearized truncation lemma

nodes.name: linearized truncation
nodes.statement_short: Weak-type bound for the operator $T_{2,\sigma_1,\sigma_2}$ summing $K_s$ over the measurable scale range $[\sigma_1(x),\sigma_2(x)]$.
assumptions: $\sigma_1,\sigma_2\colon X\to \mathbb{Z}$ be measurable functions with finite range and $\sigma_1\leq \sigma_2$
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma_1,\sigma_2\colon X\to \mathbb{Z}$ be measurable functions with finite range and $\sigma_1\leq \sigma_2$. Then we have \begin{equation} \int \mathbf{1}_{G}(x) \left| {T}_{2,\sigma_1,\sigma_2}f(x)\right|\, d\mu(x) \le \frac{2^{442a^3+2}}{(q-1)^6} \mu(G)^{1-\frac{1}{q}} \mu(F)^{\frac{1}{q}}, \end{equation} with \begin{equation} {T}_{2,\sigma_1,\sigma_2}f(x)=\sum_{\sigma_1(x) \le s\le \sigma_2(x)} \int K_s(x,y) f(y) e({Q}(x)(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y)\,. \end{equation}
nodes.label: linearized-truncation

nodes.name: Linearized truncation estimate
nodes.statement: \int \mathbf{1}_{G}(x) \left| {T}_{2,\sigma_1,\sigma_2}f(x)\right|\, d\mu(x) \le \frac{2^{442a^3+2}}{(q-1)^6} \mu(G)^{1-\frac{1}{q}} \mu(F)^{\frac{1}{q}},
nodes.label: Sqlin

nodes.name: Operator $T_{2,\sigma_1,\sigma_2}$
nodes.statement: {T}_{2,\sigma_1,\sigma_2}f(x)=\sum_{\sigma_1(x) \le s\le \sigma_2(x)} \int K_s(x,y) f(y) e({Q}(x)(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y)\,.
nodes.label: middles1

nodes.name: Proof of the linearized truncation lemma
nodes.statement_short: Apply finitary Carleson recursively to get nested exceptional sets $G_n$, sum the geometric series, and pass to the limit by monotone convergence.
nodes.statement: Fix $\sigma_1$, $\sigma_2$ and ${Q}$ as in the lemma. Applying \Cref{finitary-Carleson} recursively, we obtain a sequence of sets $G_n$ with $G_0=G$ and, for each $n\ge 0$, $G_{n+1} \subset G_n$, $\mu(G_{n})\le 2^{-n} \mu(G)$ and \begin{equation*} \int \mathbf{1}_{G_{n}\setminus G_{n+1}}(x) \left| {T}_{2,\sigma_1,\sigma_2} f(x) \right|\, d\mu(x) \end{equation*} \begin{equation} \le \frac{2^{442a^3}}{(q-1)^5} \mu(G_n)^{1 - \frac{1}{q}} \mu(F)^{\frac{1}{q}}. \end{equation} Adding the first $n$ of these inequalities, we obtain by bounding a geometric series \begin{equation} \int \mathbf{1}_{G\setminus G_{n}}(x) \left| {T}_{2,\sigma_1,\sigma_2}f(x) \right|\, d\mu(x) \le \frac{2^{442a^3+2}}{(q-1)^6} \mu(G)^{1-\frac{1}{q}} \mu(F)^{\frac{1}{q}}. \end{equation} As the integrand is non-negative and non-decreasing in $n$, we obtain by the monotone convergence theorem \begin{equation} \int \mathbf{1}_{G}(x) \left| {T}_{2,\sigma_1,\sigma_2}f(x) \right|\, d\mu(x) \le \frac{2^{442a^3+2}}{(q-1)^6} \mu(G)^{1-\frac{1}{q}} \mu(F)^{\frac{1}{q}}. \end{equation} This completes the proof of \Cref{linearized-truncation} and thus \Cref{metric-space-Carleson}.

nodes.name: Recursive application
nodes.statement_short: Iterate finitary Carleson to get sets $G_n$

nodes.name: Geometric series
nodes.statement:
Adding the first $n$ of these inequalities, we obtain by bounding a geometric series
    \begin{equation} \int \mathbf{1}_{G\setminus G_{n}}(x)
\left| {T}_{2,\sigma_1,\sigma_2}f(x) \right|\, d\mu(x)
\le \frac{2^{442a^3+2}}{(q-1)^6} \mu(G)^{1-\frac{1}{q}} \mu(F)^{\frac{1}{q}}.
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Sum a geometric series

nodes.name: Bound on $G\setminus G_n$
nodes.statement: \int \mathbf{1}_{G\setminus G_{n}}(x) \left| {T}_{2,\sigma_1,\sigma_2}f(x) \right|\, d\mu(x) \le \frac{2^{442a^3+2}}{(q-1)^6} \mu(G)^{1-\frac{1}{q}} \mu(F)^{\frac{1}{q}}.
nodes.label: Sqcut2

nodes.name: Monotone limit
nodes.statement:
As the integrand is non-negative and non-decreasing in $n$, we obtain by the monotone convergence theorem
 \begin{equation} \int \mathbf{1}_{G}(x)
\left| {T}_{2,\sigma_1,\sigma_2}f(x) \right|\, d\mu(x)
\le \frac{2^{442a^3+2}}{(q-1)^6} \mu(G)^{1-\frac{1}{q}} \mu(F)^{\frac{1}{q}}.
\end{equation}
This completes the proof of \Cref{linearized-truncation}
and thus \Cref{metric-space-Carleson}.
nodes.statement_short: Monotone convergence in $n$

nodes.name: Limit bound on $G$
nodes.statement: \int \mathbf{1}_{G}(x) \left| {T}_{2,\sigma_1,\sigma_2}f(x) \right|\, d\mu(x) \le \frac{2^{442a^3+2}}{(q-1)^6} \mu(G)^{1-\frac{1}{q}} \mu(F)^{\frac{1}{q}}.
nodes.label: Sqcut3

nodes.name: grid existence
nodes.statement_short: A grid structure of dyadic cubes exists on $X$.
conclusions: There exists a grid structure $(\mathcal{D}, c,s)$
nodes.statement: There exists a grid structure $(\mathcal{D}, c,s)$.
nodes.label: grid-existence

nodes.name: tile structure
nodes.statement_short: Every grid structure admits a tile structure.
assumptions: For a given grid structure $(\mathcal{D}, c,s)$
nodes.statement: For a given grid structure $(\mathcal{D}, c,s)$, there exists a tile structure $({\mathfrak P},{\mathcal{I}},{\Omega},{\mathcal{Q}},{\mathrm{c}},{\mathrm{s}})$.
nodes.label: tile-structure

nodes.name: Chosen grid and tile structure
nodes.statement:
Choose a grid structure $(\mathcal{D}, c,s)$ with \Cref{grid-existence} and a tile structure for this
grid structure $({\mathfrak P},{\mathcal{I}},{\Omega},{\mathcal{Q}},{\mathrm{c}},{\mathrm{s}})$ with \Cref{tile-structure}.
nodes.definiendum: grid structure $(\mathcal{D}, c,s)$ and tile structure $({\mathfrak P},{\mathcal{I}},{\Omega},{\mathcal{Q}},{\mathrm{c}},{\mathrm{s}})$

nodes.name: Exceptional set $G'$
nodes.statement:
Applying \Cref{discrete-Carleson}, we obtain a Borel set $G'$ in $X$ with $2\mu(G')\leq \mu(G)$ such that for all Borel functions $f:X\to \mathbb{C}$ with $|f|\le \mathbf{1}_F$
we have \eqref{disclesssim}.

nodes.name: tile sum operator
nodes.statement_short: Off the exceptional set, the sum of tile operators $T_{\mathfrak p}$ equals the linearised kernel sum over scales $[\sigma_1(x),\sigma_2(x)]$.
conclusions: \sum_{{\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak P}}T_{{\mathfrak p}} f(x)= \sum_{s=\sigma_1(x)}^{\sigma_2(x)} \int K_{s}(x,y) f(y) e({Q}(x)(y)-{Q}(x)(x))\, d\mu(y).
nodes.statement: We have for all $x\in G\setminus G'$ \begin{equation} \sum_{{\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak P}}T_{{\mathfrak p}} f(x)= \sum_{s=\sigma_1(x)}^{\sigma_2(x)} \int K_{s}(x,y) f(y) e({Q}(x)(y)-{Q}(x)(x))\, d\mu(y). \end{equation}
nodes.label: tile-sum-operator

nodes.name: Tile sum identity
nodes.statement: \sum_{{\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak P}}T_{{\mathfrak p}} f(x)= \sum_{s=\sigma_1(x)}^{\sigma_2(x)} \int K_{s}(x,y) f(y) e({Q}(x)(y)-{Q}(x)(x))\, d\mu(y).
nodes.label: eq-sump

nodes.name: Proof of the tile sum operator lemma
nodes.statement_short: Sort tiles by scale; at scales outside $[\sigma_1,\sigma_2]$ all $E(\mathfrak p)$ miss $x$, and inside there is exactly one tile with $x\in E(\mathfrak p)$.
nodes.statement:
Fix $x\in G\setminus G'$. Sorting the tiles ${\mathfrak p}$ on the left-hand-side of \eqref{eq-sump} by the value ${\mathrm{s}}({\mathfrak p})\in [-S,S]$, it suffices to prove for every $-S\le s\le S$ that  egin{equation} \sum_{{\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak P}: {\mathrm{s}}({\mathfrak p})=s}T_{{\mathfrak p}} f(x)=0 \end{equation} if $s
ot\in [\sigma_1(x), \sigma_2(x)]$ and  egin{equation} \sum_{{\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak P}: {\mathrm{s}}({\mathfrak p})=s}T_{{\mathfrak p}} f(x)= \int K_{s}(x,y) f(y) e({Q}(x)(y) - {Q}(x)(x))\, d\mu(y). \end{equation} if $s\in [\sigma_1(x),\sigma_2(x)]$. If $s
ot\in [\sigma_1(x), \sigma_2(x)]$, then by definition of $E({\mathfrak p})$ we have $x
ot\in E({\mathfrak p})$ for any ${\mathfrak p}$ with ${\mathrm{s}}({\mathfrak p})=s$ and thus $T_{{\mathfrak p}} f(x)=0$. This proves \eqref{outsump}. Now assume $s\in [\sigma_1(x),\sigma_2(x)]$. By \eqref{coverdyadic}, \eqref{subsetmaxcube}, \eqref{eq-vol-sp-cube}, the fact that $c(I_0) = o$ and $G\subset B(o, rac 14 D^S)$, there is at least one $I\in \mathcal{D}$ with $s(I)=s$ and $x\in I$. By \eqref{dyadicproperty}, this $I$ is unique. By \eqref{eq-dis-freq-cover}, there is precisely one ${\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak P}(I)$ such that ${Q}(x)\in {\Omega}({\mathfrak p})$. Hence there is precisely one ${\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak P}$ with ${\mathrm{s}}({\mathfrak p})=s$ such that $x\in E({\mathfrak p})$. For this ${\mathfrak p}$, the value $T_{{\mathfrak p}}(x)$ by its definition in \eqref{definetp} equals the right-hand side of \eqref{insump}. This proves the lemma.

nodes.name: Scale reduction
nodes.statement:
Fix $x\in G\setminus G'$.
    Sorting the tiles ${\mathfrak p}$ on the left-hand-side of \eqref{eq-sump} by the value ${\mathrm{s}}({\mathfrak p})\in [-S,S]$,
    it suffices to prove for every $-S\le s\le S$ that
    \begin{equation} \sum_{{\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak P}: {\mathrm{s}}({\mathfrak p})=s}T_{{\mathfrak p}} f(x)=0
    \end{equation}
    if $s\not\in [\sigma_1(x), \sigma_2(x)]$ and
    \begin{equation} \sum_{{\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak P}: {\mathrm{s}}({\mathfrak p})=s}T_{{\mathfrak p}} f(x)=
        \int K_{s}(x,y) f(y) e({Q}(x)(y) - {Q}(x)(x))\, d\mu(y).
    \end{equation}
    if $s\in [\sigma_1(x),\sigma_2(x)]$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a scale-by-scale identity

nodes.name: Vanishing outside the scale range
nodes.statement: \sum_{{\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak P}: {\mathrm{s}}({\mathfrak p})=s}T_{{\mathfrak p}} f(x)=0
nodes.label: outsump

nodes.name: Tile sum at a single scale
nodes.statement: \sum_{{\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak P}: {\mathrm{s}}({\mathfrak p})=s}T_{{\mathfrak p}} f(x)= \int K_{s}(x,y) f(y) e({Q}(x)(y) - {Q}(x)(x))\, d\mu(y).
nodes.label: insump

nodes.name: Outside scales
nodes.statement:
If $s\not\in [\sigma_1(x), \sigma_2(x)]$, then by definition of $E({\mathfrak p})$ we have
    $x\not\in E({\mathfrak p})$ for any ${\mathfrak p}$ with ${\mathrm{s}}({\mathfrak p})=s$ and thus $T_{{\mathfrak p}} f(x)=0$. This proves
    \eqref{outsump}.
nodes.statement_short: Scales outside the range contribute zero

nodes.name: Inside scales
nodes.statement:
Now assume $s\in [\sigma_1(x),\sigma_2(x)]$.
    By \eqref{coverdyadic}, \eqref{subsetmaxcube}, \eqref{eq-vol-sp-cube}, the fact that $c(I_0) = o$ and $G\subset B(o,\frac 14 D^S)$, there is at least
    one $I\in \mathcal{D}$ with $s(I)=s$ and $x\in I$.
nodes.statement_short: Find a cube of scale $s$ containing $x$

nodes.name: Unique cube
nodes.statement: By \eqref{dyadicproperty}, this $I$ is unique.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness of the cube

nodes.name: Unique tile
nodes.statement:
By \eqref{eq-dis-freq-cover}, there is precisely one ${\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak P}(I)$ such that
    ${Q}(x)\in {\Omega}({\mathfrak p})$. Hence there is precisely one ${\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak P}$ with ${\mathrm{s}}({\mathfrak p})=s$ such that
    $x\in E({\mathfrak p})$.
nodes.statement_short: Exactly one tile has $x\in E(\mathfrak p)$

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement:
For this ${\mathfrak p}$, the value $T_{{\mathfrak p}}(x)$ by its definition in \eqref{definetp}
    equals the right-hand side of \eqref{insump}. This proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Its operator gives the right-hand side

nodes.name: Proof of finitary Carleson
nodes.statement_short: Combine the tile sum identity with the discrete Carleson bound.
nodes.statement: We now estimate with \Cref{tile-sum-operator} and \Cref{discrete-Carleson} \begin{equation} \int_{G \setminus G'} \left|\sum_{s={\sigma_1}(x)}^{{\sigma_2}(x)} \int K_s(x,y) f(y) e({Q}(x)(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y)\right| \mathrm{d}\mu(x) \end{equation} \begin{equation} =\int_{G \setminus G'} \left|\sum_{s={\sigma_1}(x)}^{{\sigma_2}(x)} \int K_s(x,y) f(y) e({Q}(x)(y) - {Q}(x)(x))\mathrm{d}\mu(y)\right| \mathrm{d}\mu(x) \end{equation} \begin{equation} =\int_{G \setminus G'} \left|\sum_{{\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak P}}T_{{\mathfrak p}} f(x)\right| \mathrm{d}\mu(x) \le \frac{2^{442a^3}}{(q-1)^5} \mu(G)^{1 - \frac{1}{q}} \mu(F)^{\frac{1}{q}} \,. \end{equation} This proves \eqref{eq-linearized} for the chosen set $G'$ and arbitrary $f$ and thus completes the proof of Proposition \ref{finitary-Carleson}.

nodes.name: Finitary Carleson left-hand side
nodes.statement: \int_{G \setminus G'} \left|\sum_{s={\sigma_1}(x)}^{{\sigma_2}(x)} \int K_s(x,y) f(y) e({Q}(x)(y)) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y)\right| \mathrm{d}\mu(x)

nodes.name: Phase-shifted left-hand side
nodes.statement: =\int_{G \setminus G'} \left|\sum_{s={\sigma_1}(x)}^{{\sigma_2}(x)} \int K_s(x,y) f(y) e({Q}(x)(y) - {Q}(x)(x))\mathrm{d}\mu(y)\right| \mathrm{d}\mu(x)

nodes.name: Tile sum bound by discrete Carleson
nodes.statement: =\int_{G \setminus G'} \left|\sum_{{\mathfrak p}\in {\mathfrak P}}T_{{\mathfrak p}} f(x)\right| \mathrm{d}\mu(x) \le \frac{2^{442a^3}}{(q-1)^5} \mu(G)^{1 - \frac{1}{q}} \mu(F)^{\frac{1}{q}} \,.

nodes.name: counting balls
nodes.statement_short: A $D^k$-separated set of centres in $B(o,4D^S)$ has at most $2^{3a+200Sa^3}$ points.
assumptions: Consider $Y\subset X$ such that for any $y\in Y$, we have \begin{equation} y\in B(o,4D^S-D^k), \end{equation}
furthermore, for any $y'\in Y$ with $y\neq y'$, we have \begin{equation} B(y,D^k)\cap B(y',D^k)=\emptyset. \end{equation}
conclusions: Then the cardinality of $Y$ is bounded by \begin{equation} |Y|\le 2^{3a + 200Sa^3}\, . \end{equation}
nodes.statement: Let $-S\le k\le S$. Consider $Y\subset X$ such that for any $y\in Y$, we have \begin{equation} y\in B(o,4D^S-D^k), \end{equation} furthermore, for any $y'\in Y$ with $y\neq y'$, we have \begin{equation} B(y,D^k)\cap B(y',D^k)=\emptyset. \end{equation} Then the cardinality of $Y$ is bounded by \begin{equation} |Y|\le 2^{3a + 200Sa^3}\, . \end{equation}
nodes.label: counting-balls

nodes.name: Centres in the ball
nodes.statement: y\in B(o,4D^S-D^k),
nodes.label: ybinb

nodes.name: Disjoint balls around centres
nodes.statement: B(y,D^k)\cap B(y',D^k)=\emptyset.
nodes.label: eq-disj-yballs

nodes.name: Proof of the counting balls lemma
nodes.statement_short: Volume counting: by doubling each small ball has measure comparable to $B(o,4D^S)$, and the balls are disjoint.
nodes.statement: Let $k$ and $Y$ be given. By applying the doubling property \eqref{doublingx} inductively, we have for each integer $j\ge 0$ \begin{equation} \mu(B(y,2^{j}D^k))\le 2^{aj} \mu(B(y,D^k))\, . \end{equation} Since $X$ is the union of the balls $B(y,2^{j}D^k)$ and $\mu$ is not zero, at least one of the balls $B(y,2^{j}D^k)$ has positive measure, thus $B(y,D^k)$ has positive measure. Applying \eqref{jballs} for $j' = \ln_2(8D^{2S}) = 3 + 2S \cdot 100a^2$ by \eqref{defineD}, using $-S\le k\le S$, $y\in B(o,4D^S)$, and the triangle inequality, we have \begin{equation} B(o, 4D^S) \subset B(y, 8D^S) \subset B(y,2^{j'}D^k) \, . \end{equation} Using the disjointedness of the balls in \eqref{eq-disj-yballs}, \eqref{ybinb}, and the triangle inequality for $\rho$, we obtain \begin{equation} |Y|\mu(B(o,4D^S))\le 2^{j'a}\sum_{y\in Y}\mu(B(y,D^k)) \end{equation} \begin{equation} \le 2^{j'a}\mu(\bigcup_{y\in Y}B(y,D^k)) \le 2^{j'a}\mu(o,4D^S)\, . \end{equation} As $\mu(o,4D^S)$ is not zero, the lemma follows.

nodes.name: Iterated doubling
nodes.statement_short: Iterate the doubling property

nodes.name: Positive measure
nodes.statement: Since $X$ is the union of the balls $B(y,2^{j}D^k)$ and $\mu$ is not zero, at least one of the balls $B(y,2^{j}D^k)$ has positive measure, thus $B(y,D^k)$ has positive measure.
nodes.statement_short: Each small ball has positive measure

nodes.name: Containment
nodes.statement_short: Big ball is inside a dilate of each small ball

nodes.name: Ball containment
nodes.statement: B(o, 4D^S) \subset B(y, 8D^S) \subset B(y,2^{j'}D^k) \, .

nodes.name: Volume count
nodes.statement_short: Sum over disjoint balls

nodes.name: Measure count
nodes.statement: |Y|\mu(B(o,4D^S))\le 2^{j'a}\sum_{y\in Y}\mu(B(y,D^k))

nodes.name: Measure count continued
nodes.statement: \le 2^{j'a}\mu(\bigcup_{y\in Y}B(y,D^k)) \le 2^{j'a}\mu(o,4D^S)\, .

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: As $\mu(o,4D^S)$ is not zero, the lemma follows.
nodes.statement_short: Divide by the positive measure

nodes.name: Maximal separated centre sets $Y_k$
nodes.statement:
For each $-S\le k\le S$, let $Y_k$ be a set of
maximal cardinality in $X$ such that $Y=Y_k$ satisfies
the properties \eqref{ybinb} and \eqref{eq-disj-yballs} and such that $o \in Y_k$.
By the upper bound of \Cref{counting-balls}, such a set exists.
nodes.statement_short: $Y_k$: a maximal set of $D^k$-separated centres in $B(o,4D^S-D^k)$ containing $o$; it exists by the counting balls lemma.

nodes.name: Total order on $Y_k$
nodes.statement:
For each $-S\le k\le S$, choose an enumeration of the points in the finite set $Y_k$ and thus a total
order $<$ on $Y_{k}$.

nodes.name: cover big ball
nodes.statement_short: Balls of radius $2D^k$ around the points of $Y_k$ cover $B(o,4D^S-D^k)$.
conclusions: the ball $B(o, 4D^S-D^k)$ is contained in the union of the balls $B(y,2D^k)$ with $y\in Y_k$
nodes.statement: For each $-S\le k\le S$, the ball $B(o, 4D^S-D^k)$ is contained in the union of the balls $B(y,2D^k)$ with $y\in Y_k$.
nodes.label: cover-big-ball

nodes.name: Proof of the cover big ball lemma
nodes.statement_short: By maximality of $Y_k$, every ball $B(x,D^k)$ meets some $B(y,D^k)$; conclude by the triangle inequality.
nodes.statement: Let $x$ be any point of $B(o, 4D^S-D^k)$. By maximality of $|Y_k|$, the ball $B(x, D^k)$ intersects one of the balls $B(y, D^k)$ with $y\in Y_k$. By the triangle inequality, $x\in B(y,2D^k)$.

nodes.name: Maximality
nodes.statement:
Let $x$ be any point of $B(o, 4D^S-D^k)$. By maximality of $|Y_k|$, the ball
$B(x, D^k)$ intersects one of the balls
$B(y, D^k)$ with $y\in Y_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Maximality gives an intersecting centre ball

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement:
By the triangle
inequality, $x\in B(y,2D^k)$.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality

nodes.name: Index set $\mathcal{C}$
Index set $\mathcal{C}$
nodes.statement: \mathcal{C}:= \{(y,k): -S\le k\le S, y\in Y_k\}\,

nodes.name: Lexicographic order on $\mathcal{C}$
nodes.statement:
We totally order the set $\mathcal{C}$ lexicographically by setting
$(y,k)<(y',k')$ if $k< k'$ or both $k=k'$ and $y<y'$.

nodes.name: Sets $I_1(y,k)$ and $I_2(y,k)$
nodes.statement:
In what follows, we define recursively in the sense of this order a function
\begin{equation}
    (I_1,I_2,I_3): \mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{P}(X)\times \mathcal{P}(X)\times \mathcal{P}(X)\, .
\end{equation}


Assume the sets ${I}_j(y',k')$ have already been defined for $j=1,2,3$ if $k'<k$ and if $k=k'$ and $y'<y$.




If $k=-S$, define for $j\in \{1,2\}$ the set
${I}_j(y,k)$ to be $B(y,jD^{-S})$.
If $-S<k$, define for $j\in \{1,2\}$
and $y\in Y_k$ the set ${I}_j(y,k)$ to be
\begin{equation} \bigcup\{I_3(y',k-1):
y'\in Y_{k-1}\cap B(y,jD^k)\}.
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Recursive definition: at the bottom scale $I_j(y,-S)=B(y,jD^{-S})$; above, $I_j(y,k)$ is the union of the $I_3$-cubes of the previous scale with centres in $B(y,jD^k)$.

nodes.name: The map $(I_1,I_2,I_3)$
nodes.statement: (I_1,I_2,I_3): \mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{P}(X)\times \mathcal{P}(X)\times \mathcal{P}(X)\, .

nodes.name: Definition of $I_j(y,k)$ (defineij)
nodes.statement: \bigcup\{I_3(y',k-1): y'\in Y_{k-1}\cap B(y,jD^k)\}.
nodes.label: defineij

nodes.name: Dyadic cube $I_3(y,k)$
nodes.statement_short: $I_3(y,k)$ is $I_1(y,k)$ together with the part of $I_2(y,k)$ not in $X_k$ or in earlier $I_3(y',k)$; $X_k$ is the union of all $I_1(y',k)$.

nodes.name: Definition of $I_3(y,k)$ (definei3)
nodes.statement: I_3(y,k):={I_1}(y,k)\cup \left[{I_2}(y,k)\setminus \left[X_k\cup \bigcup\{I_3(y',k):y'\in Y_{k}, y'<y\})\right]\right]
nodes.label: definei3

nodes.name: Set $X_k$
nodes.statement: X_{k}:=\bigcup\{I_1(y', k):y'\in Y_{k}\}.

nodes.name: basic grid structure
nodes.statement_short: Disjointness of the $I_1$ and $I_3$ cubes at one scale, covering of $B(o,4D^S-2D^k)$ by the $I_2$ and $I_3$ cubes, and $B(y,\frac12D^k)\subset I_3(y,k)\subset B(y,4D^k)$.
assumptions: For each $-S\le k\le S$ and $1\le j\le 3$
$j\neq 2$ and for some $x\in X$ and $y_1,y_2\in Y_k$ we have \begin{equation} x\in I_j(y_1,k)\cap I_j(y_2,k), \end{equation}
conclusions: We have for each $y\in Y_k$, \begin{equation} B(y,\frac 12 D^k) \subset I_3(y,k)\subset B(y,4D^k). \end{equation}

assumptions: $j\neq 2$ and for some $x\in X$ and $y_1,y_2\in Y_k$ we have \begin{equation} x\in I_j(y_1,k)\cap I_j(y_2,k), \end{equation}

conclusions: We have for each $y\in Y_k$, \begin{equation} B(y,\frac 12 D^k) \subset I_3(y,k)\subset B(y,4D^k). \end{equation}

nodes.statement: For each $-S\le k\le S$ and $1\le j\le 3$ the following holds. If $j\neq 2$ and for some $x\in X$ and $y_1,y_2\in Y_k$ we have \begin{equation} x\in I_j(y_1,k)\cap I_j(y_2,k), \end{equation} then $y_1=y_2$. If $j\neq 1$, then \begin{equation} B(o, 4D^S-2D^k)\subset \bigcup_{y\in Y_k} I_j(y,k)\, . \end{equation} We have for each $y\in Y_k$, \begin{equation} B(y,\frac 12 D^k) \subset I_3(y,k)\subset B(y,4D^k). \end{equation}
nodes.label: basic-grid-structure

nodes.name: Disjointness at one scale (disji)
nodes.statement: x\in I_j(y_1,k)\cap I_j(y_2,k),
nodes.label: disji

nodes.name: Covering at one scale (unioni)
nodes.statement: B(o, 4D^S-2D^k)\subset \bigcup_{y\in Y_k} I_j(y,k)\, .
nodes.label: unioni

nodes.name: Squeezing property (squeezedyadic)
nodes.statement: B(y,\frac 12 D^k) \subset I_3(y,k)\subset B(y,4D^k).
nodes.label: squeezedyadic

nodes.name: Proof of the basic grid structure lemma
nodes.statement_short: Simultaneous induction over the ordered pairs $(y,k)$, proving disjointness, covering and squeezing from the recursive definitions.
nodes.statement: We prove these statements simultaneously by induction on the ordered set of pairs $(y,k)$. Let $-S\le k\le S$. We first consider \eqref{disji} for $j=1$. If $k=-S$, disjointedness of the sets $I_1(y,-S)$ follows by definition of $I_1$ and $Y_k$. If $k>-S$, assume $x$ is in $I_1(y_m,k)$ for $m=1,2$. Then, for $m=1,2$, there is $z_m\in Y_{k-1}\cap B(y_m,D^k)$ with $x\in I_3(z_m,k-1)$. Using \eqref{disji} inductively for $j=3$, we conclude $z_1=z_2$. This implies that the balls $B(y_1, D^k)$ and $B(y_2, D^k)$ intersect. By construction of $Y_k$, this implies $y_1=y_2$. This proves \eqref{disji} for $j=1$. We next consider \eqref{disji} for $j=3$. Assume $x$ is in $I_3(y_m,k)$ for $m=1,2$ and $y_m\in Y_k$. If $x$ is in $X_k$, then by definition \eqref{definei3}, $x\in I_1(y_m,k)$ for $m=1,2$. As we have already shown \eqref{disji} for $j=1$, we conclude $y_1=y_2$. This completes the proof in case $x\in X_k$, and we may assume $x$ is not in $X_k$. By definition \eqref{definei3}, $x$ is not in $I_3(z,k)$ for any $z$ with $z<y_1$ or $z<y_2$. Hence, neither $y_1<y_2$ nor $y_2<y_1$, and by totality of the order of $Y_k$, we have $y_1=y_2$. This completes the proof of \eqref{disji} for $j=3$. We show \eqref{unioni} for $j=2$. In case $k=-S$, this follows from \Cref{cover-big-ball}. Assume $k>-S$. Let $x$ be a point of $B(o, 4D^S-2D^k)$. By induction, there is $y'\in Y_{k-1}$ such that $x\in I_3(y',k-1)$. Using the inductive statement \eqref{squeezedyadic}, we obtain $x\in B(y',4D^{k-1})$. As $D>4$, by applying the triangle inequality with the points, $o$, $x$, and $y'$, we obtain that $y'\in B(o, 4D^S-D^k)$. By \Cref{cover-big-ball}, $y'$ is in $B(y,2D^k)$ for some $y\in Y_k$. It follows that $x\in I_2(y,k)$. This proves \eqref{unioni} for $j=2$. We show \eqref{unioni} for $j=3$. Let $x\in B(o, 4D^S-2D^k)$. In case $x\in X_k$, then by definition of $X_k$ we have $x\in I_1(y,k)$ for some $y\in Y_k$ and thus $x\in I_3(y,k)$. We may thus assume $x\not\in X_k$. As we have already seen \eqref{unioni} for $j=2$, there is $y\in Y_k$ such that $x\in I_2(y,k)$. We may assume this $y$ is minimal with respect to the order in $Y_k$. Then $x\in I_3(y,k)$. This proves \eqref{unioni} for $j=3$. Next, we show the first inclusion in \eqref{squeezedyadic}. Let $x\in B(y,\frac 12 D^k)$. As $I_1(y,k)\subset I_3(y,k)$, it suffices to show $x\in I_1(y,k)$. If $k=-S$, this follows immediately from the assumption on $x$ and the definition of $I_1$. Assume $k>-S$. By the inductive statement \eqref{unioni} and $D>4$, there is a $y'\in Y_{k-1}$ such that $x\in I_3(y',k-1)$. By the inductive statement \eqref{squeezedyadic}, we conclude $x\in B(y',4D^{k-1})$. By the triangle inequality with points $x$, $y$, $y'$, and $D\geq8$, we have $y'\in B(y,D^k)$. It follows by definition \eqref{defineij} that $I_3(y',k-1)\subset I_1(y,k)$, and thus $x\in I_3(y,k)$. This proves the first inclusion in \eqref{squeezedyadic}. We show the second inclusion in \eqref{squeezedyadic}. Let $x\in I_3(y,k)$.
