nodes.name: Constant c and alpha'
Proof of the weak (1,1) bound, trivial case
nodes.statement:
If $\alpha'\le\frac{1}{\mu(X)}\int |f|\,d\mu$, then we directly have
\begin{equation*}
    \mu\left(\{x\in X: |T_r f(x)|>\alpha\}\right)\le \mu(X) \le \frac{1}{\alpha'} \int |f(y)|\, d\mu(y)
    \le \frac{2^{a^3 + 19a}}{\alpha} \int |f(y)|\, d\mu(y),
\end{equation*}
which proves \eqref{eq-weak-1-1}.
So assume from now on that $\alpha'>\frac{1}{\mu(X)}\int |f|\,d\mu$.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial case $\alpha'\le$ average of $|f|$: bound by $\mu(X)$; otherwise reduce to $\alpha'$ above the average.

nodes.name: Good and bad parts g, b for the weak (1,1) proof
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Calderón-Zygmund decomposition to $f$ at height $\alpha'$: $f=g+b=g+\sum_j b_j$.

nodes.name: Balls B_{3,j} of the decomposition
nodes.statement:
Let
\begin{equation} B_{3,j}=B(x_j, 3r_j)
\end{equation}
as in the lemma.

nodes.name: Balls B_{6,j}
nodes.statement_short: $B_{6,j}=B(x_j,6r_j)$, concentric with $B_{3,j}$, with $\mu(B_{6,j})\le 2^a\mu(B_{3,j})$.

nodes.name: Exceptional set Omega
Omega as union of B_{6,j}
nodes.statement: \Omega:=\bigcup_j B_{6,j}.
nodes.label: eq-omega

nodes.name: Estimate good
nodes.statement_short: Weak-type bound for $T_r g$ on the good part via the $L^2$ bound of $T_r$.
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \mu\left(\{x\in X: |T_r g(x)|>{\alpha}/2\}\right) \le \frac{2^{2a^3+3a+2}c}{\alpha} \int |f(y)|\, d\mu(y). \end{equation*}
nodes.label: estimate-good

nodes.name: Proof of Estimate good
nodes.statement_short: Chebyshev's inequality, then the $L^2$ bound of $T_r$ and the $L^\infty$/$L^1$ bounds on $g$.
nodes.statement: We estimate using monotonicity of the integral \begin{equation*} \mu\left(\{x\in X: |T_r g(x)|>{\alpha}/2\}\right)\leq \frac{4}{\alpha^2} \int |T_r g(y)|^2\, d\mu(y). \end{equation*} Using \eqref{eq-strong-2-2-assumption} followed by \eqref{eq-g-max} and \eqref{eq-g-L1-norm}, we estimate the right hand side above by \begin{equation} \leq \frac{4\cdot 2^{2a^3}}{\alpha^2} \int |g(y)|^2\, d\mu(y)\leq \frac{2^{2a^3+3a+2}c}{\alpha} \int |g(y)|\, dy \le \frac{2^{2a^3+3a+2}c}{\alpha} \int |f(y)|\, d\mu(y). \end{equation}

nodes.name: L^2 estimate for T_r g
nodes.statement: \leq \frac{4\cdot 2^{2a^3}}{\alpha^2} \int |g(y)|^2\, d\mu(y)\leq \frac{2^{2a^3+3a+2}c}{\alpha} \int |g(y)|\, dy \le \frac{2^{2a^3+3a+2}c}{\alpha} \int |f(y)|\, d\mu(y).
nodes.label: eq-Hr-g

nodes.name: Estimate bad partial
nodes.statement_short: Off $\Omega$, $|T_r b|$ is bounded by $3F(x)+\alpha/8$ for an explicit kernel-weighted sum $F$.
nodes.statement: Let $x\in X\setminus\Omega$. Then \begin{equation*} |T_rb(x)| \le 3F(x)+\alpha/8, \end{equation*} where \begin{equation*} F(x) := 2^{a^3+2a+1} c\alpha \sum_{j\in J} \left(\frac{3r_j}{\rho(x,x_j)}\right)^{\frac{1}{a}}\frac{\mu(B_{3,j})}{V(x,x_j)}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: estimate-bad-partial

nodes.name: Proof of Estimate bad partial
nodes.statement_short: Split indices $j$ by position of $B_{3,j}$ relative to $B(x,r)$; far balls use mean zero and kernel smoothness, boundary balls lie in an annulus. Key step: the boundary balls' union is in $B(x,3r)\setminus B(x,r/3)$.
nodes.statement: We decompose the index set $J$ into the following disjoint sets: \begin{align*} \mathcal{J}_1(x)&:=\{j\,: r+3r_j \le \rho(x,x_j) \},\\ \mathcal{J}_2(x)&:=\{j\,: r-3r_j \le \rho(x,x_j) < r+3r_j\},\\ \mathcal{J}_3(x)&:=\{j\,: \rho(x,x_j) < r-3r_j\}. \end{align*} Then \begin{alignat}{3} |T_r b(x)|\le&&&\sum_{j\in \mathcal{J}_1(x)} |T_rb_j(x)| \\ &+&&\sum_{j\in \mathcal{J}_2(x)} |T_rb_j(x)| \\ &+&&\sum_{j\in \mathcal{J}_3(x)} |T_rb_j(x)|. \end{alignat} For all $j\in \mathcal{J}_3(x)$, $\operatorname{supp} b_j\subset B_{3,j}\subset B(x,r)$, and thus $T_rb_j(x)=0$, so $\eqref{eq-b-dec-3} = 0$. Next, for $j\in \mathcal{J}_1(x)$, $\operatorname{supp} b_j\subset B_{3,j}\subset X \setminus B(x,r)$, and we have \begin{equation*} T_rb_j(x)=\int_{X\setminus B(x,r)} K(x,y) b_j(y)\,d\mu(y)=\int_{B_{3,j}} K(x,y) b_j(y)\,d\mu(y)\,. \end{equation*} Using \eqref{eq-bad-mean-zero}, the above is equal to \begin{equation*} \int_{{3,j}} (K(x,y)-K(x,x_j)) b_j(y)\,d\mu(y)\,. \end{equation*} Since $x\in X\setminus\Omega$, we have for each $y\in B_{3,j}$ that \begin{equation} \rho(x,x_j)\ge 6r_j > 2\rho(x_j,y), \end{equation} so we can apply \eqref{eqkernel-y-smooth} to estimate \begin{equation*} \eqref{eq-b-dec-1} \le \sum_{j\in \mathcal{J}_1(x)}\int_{B_{3,j}}\left(\frac{\rho(x_j,y)}{\rho(x,x_j)}\right)^{\frac{1}{a}}\frac{2^{a^3}}{V(x,x_j)} |b_j(y)|\, d\mu(y) \end{equation*} \begin{equation} \le 2^{a^3} \sum_{j} \left(\frac{3r_j}{\rho(x,x_j)}\right)^{\frac{1}{a}}\frac{1}{V(x,x_j)}\int_{B_{3,j}} |b_j(y)|\, dy \end{equation} and by \eqref{eq-bj-L1}, \begin{equation} \le 2^{a^3+2a+1} c\alpha \sum_{j} \left(\frac{3r_j}{\rho(x,x_j)}\right)^{\frac{1}{a}}\frac{\mu(B_{3,j})}{V(x,x_j)} = F(x). \end{equation} Next, we estimate \eqref{eq-b-dec-2}. For each $j\in \mathcal{J}_2(x)$, set \begin{equation*} d_j:=\frac{1}{\mu(B_{3,j})}\int_{B_{3,j}} \mathbf{1}_{X\setminus B(x,r)}(y) b_j(y)\, dy. \end{equation*} Then by \eqref{eq-bj-L1} \begin{equation} |d_j|\le 2^{2a+1} c\alpha. \end{equation} For each $j\in \mathcal{J}_2(x)$, we have \begin{align*} T_r b_j(x)&=\int_{B_{3,j}} K(x,y) (\mathbf{1}_{X\setminus B(x,r)}(y)b_j(y)-d_j)\, dy + \int_{B_{3,j}} d_j K(x,y) \, dy \\ &= \int_{B_{3,j}} (K(x,y)-K(x,x_j)) (\mathbf{1}_{X\setminus B(x,r)}(y)b_j(y)-d_j)\, dy + \int_{B_{3,j}} d_j K(x,y) \, dy. \end{align*} Thus, using the triangle inequality, the equation above and \eqref{eq-dj-est}, we obtain \begin{equation*} |T_r b_j(x)|\le \end{equation*} \begin{equation} \int_{B_{3,j}} |K(x,y)-K(x,x_j)| \left(|b_j(y)|+2^{2a+1} c\alpha\right)\, dy +2^{2a+1} c\alpha \int_{B_{3,j}} |K(x,y)| \, dy. \end{equation} By \eqref{eq-Om-cj}, we can apply \eqref{eqkernel-y-smooth} and arguing as in \eqref{eq-J1-diff-est}, we get that \begin{equation} \eqref{eq-b-dec-2} \le 2F(x) + 2^{2a+1}c\alpha \sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_2(x)} \int_{B_{3,j}} |K(x,y)|\,d\mu(y), \end{equation} with $F$ as in \eqref{eq-J1-diff-est}. Define \begin{equation*} A := \bigcup_{j \in \mathcal{J}_2(x)} B_{3,j}. \end{equation*} We claim that \begin{equation} A\subset B(x,3r) \setminus B(x,\frac{r}{3}). \end{equation} Indeed, for each $j\in \mathcal{J}_2(x)$ and $y\in B_{3,j}$, using again \eqref{eq-Om-cj}, \begin{equation*} \rho(x,x_j) < r+r_{3,j} \le r + \frac{1}{2} \rho(x,x_j) \implies \rho(x,x_j) < 2r \end{equation*} and hence \begin{equation*} \rho(x,y) \le \rho(x,x_j) + \rho(x_j,y) < 2r + 3r_j \le 2r + \frac{1}{2}\rho(x,x_j) < 3r. \end{equation*} For the lower bound, we observe \begin{equation*} \rho(x,x_j) \ge r-3r_j \ge r - \frac{1}{2} \rho(x,x_j) \implies \rho(x,x_j) \ge \frac{2}{3}r, \end{equation*} and conclude \begin{equation*} \rho(x,y) \ge \rho(x,x_j) - \rho(y,x_j) \ge \rho(x,x_j) - 3r_j \ge \rho(x,x_j) - \frac{1}{2}\rho(x,x_j) \ge \frac{1}{3} r. \end{equation*} Using the bounded intersection property of the $B_{3,j}$, \eqref{eq-J2-union-subset} and \eqref{eqkernel-size}, we get \begin{align} \sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_2(x)} \int_{B_{3,j}} |K(x,y)|\,d\mu(y) &\le 2^{6a} \int_{A} |K(x,y)|\,d\mu(y) \\ &\le 2^{6a} \int_{B(x,3r) \setminus B(x,\frac{r}{3})} |K(x,y)|\,d\mu(y) \\ &\le 2^{6a} \int_{B(x,3r) \setminus B(x,\frac{r}{3})} \frac{2^{a^3}}{V(x,y)} \,d\mu(y) \\ &\le 2^{a^3+6a} \int_{B(x,3r) \setminus B(x,\frac{r}{3})} \frac{1}{\mu(B(x,\frac{r}{3}))} \,d\mu(y) \\ &\le 2^{a^3+6a} \frac{\mu(B(x,3r))}{\mu(B(x,\frac{r}{3}))} \\ &\le 2^{a^3+10a}. \end{align} If we combine the estimates \eqref{eq-J1-diff-est} for \eqref{eq-b-dec-1}, \eqref{eq-J2-diff-est-2} for \eqref{eq-b-dec-2}, and \eqref{eq-J2-diff-est-4}, we get \begin{equation*} |T_rb(x)|\leq 3F(x)+2^{a^3+12a+1}c\alpha. \end{equation*} By the definition \eqref{weak-1-1-proof-cz-const} of $c$, this equals \begin{equation*} 3F(x)+\alpha/8. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Split J into J_1, J_2, J_3 and the sum accordingly
nodes.statement_short: Split J into J_1, J_2, J_3 and the sum accordingly

nodes.name: Splitting |T_r b| over J_1, J_2, J_3
nodes.statement: {3} |T_r b(x)|\le&&&\sum_{j\in \mathcal{J}_1(x)} |T_rb_j(x)| \\ &+&&\sum_{j\in \mathcal{J}_2(x)} |T_rb_j(x)| \\ &+&&\sum_{j\in \mathcal{J}_3(x)} |T_rb_j(x)|.
nodes.label: eq-b-dec-1

nodes.name: Terms in J_3 vanish
nodes.statement: For all $j\in \mathcal{J}_3(x)$, $\operatorname{supp} b_j\subset B_{3,j}\subset B(x,r)$, and thus $T_rb_j(x)=0$, so $\eqref{eq-b-dec-3} = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Terms in J_3 vanish

nodes.name: Bound the J_1 terms by F(x) using mean zero and kernel smoothness
nodes.statement_short: Bound the J_1 terms by F(x) using mean zero and kernel smoothness

nodes.name: Rewrite T_r b_j as an integral over B_{3,j}
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite T_r b_j as an integral over B_{3,j}

nodes.name: Subtract K(x,x_j) using mean zero
nodes.statement_short: Subtract K(x,x_j) using mean zero

nodes.name: Apply kernel smoothness and the L^1 bound of b_j
nodes.statement_short: Apply kernel smoothness and the L^1 bound of b_j

nodes.name: Separation of x from the balls
nodes.statement: \rho(x,x_j)\ge 6r_j > 2\rho(x_j,y),
nodes.label: eq-Om-cj

nodes.name: Kernel smoothness bound for J_1 sum
nodes.statement: \le 2^{a^3} \sum_{j} \left(\frac{3r_j}{\rho(x,x_j)}\right)^{\frac{1}{a}}\frac{1}{V(x,x_j)}\int_{B_{3,j}} |b_j(y)|\, dy

nodes.name: J_1 sum bounded by F(x)
nodes.statement: \le 2^{a^3+2a+1} c\alpha \sum_{j} \left(\frac{3r_j}{\rho(x,x_j)}\right)^{\frac{1}{a}}\frac{\mu(B_{3,j})}{V(x,x_j)} = F(x).
nodes.label: eq-J1-diff-est

nodes.name: Bound the J_2 terms
nodes.statement_short: Bound the J_2 terms

nodes.name: Introduce the averages d_j and bound them
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the averages d_j and bound them

nodes.name: Bound on the averages d_j
nodes.statement: |d_j|\le 2^{2a+1} c\alpha.
nodes.label: eq-dj-est

nodes.name: Rewrite and bound T_r b_j for j in J_2
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite and bound T_r b_j for j in J_2

nodes.name: Estimate of T_r b_j for j in J_2
nodes.statement: \int_{B_{3,j}} |K(x,y)-K(x,x_j)| \left(|b_j(y)|+2^{2a+1} c\alpha\right)\, dy +2^{2a+1} c\alpha \int_{B_{3,j}} |K(x,y)| \, dy.
nodes.label: eq-J2-diff-est

nodes.name: Sum to bound the J_2 part by 2F(x) plus a kernel integral
nodes.statement:
By \eqref{eq-Om-cj}, we can apply \eqref{eqkernel-y-smooth} and arguing as in \eqref{eq-J1-diff-est}, we get that
\begin{equation} \eqref{eq-b-dec-2} \le 2F(x) + 2^{2a+1}c\alpha \sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_2(x)} \int_{B_{3,j}}  |K(x,y)|\,d\mu(y),
\end{equation}
with $F$ as in \eqref{eq-J1-diff-est}.
nodes.statement_short: Sum to bound the J_2 part by 2F(x) plus a kernel integral

nodes.name: J_2 sum bound
nodes.statement: \eqref{eq-b-dec-2} \le 2F(x) + 2^{2a+1}c\alpha \sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_2(x)} \int_{B_{3,j}} |K(x,y)|\,d\mu(y),
nodes.label: eq-J2-diff-est-2

nodes.name: Claim: the union A of J_2 balls lies in an annulus
nodes.statement_short: Claim: the union A of J_2 balls lies in an annulus

nodes.name: Union of J_2 balls lies in an annulus
nodes.statement: A\subset B(x,3r) \setminus B(x,\frac{r}{3}).
nodes.label: eq-J2-union-subset

nodes.name: Upper bound: points of A are within 3r
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound: points of A are within 3r

nodes.name: Lower bound: points of A are at least r/3 away
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound: points of A are at least r/3 away

nodes.name: Bound the kernel integral over the annulus by bounded overlap and kernel size
nodes.statement:
Using the bounded intersection property of the $B_{3,j}$, \eqref{eq-J2-union-subset} and \eqref{eqkernel-size}, we get
\begin{align}
    \sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_2(x)} \int_{B_{3,j}}  |K(x,y)|\,d\mu(y) &\le 2^{6a} \int_{A}  |K(x,y)|\,d\mu(y) \\
    &\le 2^{6a} \int_{B(x,3r) \setminus B(x,\frac{r}{3})}  |K(x,y)|\,d\mu(y) \\
    &\le 2^{6a} \int_{B(x,3r) \setminus B(x,\frac{r}{3})} \frac{2^{a^3}}{V(x,y)} \,d\mu(y) \\
    &\le 2^{a^3+6a} \int_{B(x,3r) \setminus B(x,\frac{r}{3})} \frac{1}{\mu(B(x,\frac{r}{3}))} \,d\mu(y) \\
    &\le 2^{a^3+6a} \frac{\mu(B(x,3r))}{\mu(B(x,\frac{r}{3}))} \\ &\le 2^{a^3+10a}.
\end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the kernel integral over the annulus by bounded overlap and kernel size

nodes.name: Kernel integral over the annulus
nodes.statement: \sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_2(x)} \int_{B_{3,j}} |K(x,y)|\,d\mu(y) &\le 2^{6a} \int_{A} |K(x,y)|\,d\mu(y) \\ &\le 2^{6a} \int_{B(x,3r) \setminus B(x,\frac{r}{3})} |K(x,y)|\,d\mu(y) \\ &\le 2^{6a} \int_{B(x,3r) \setminus B(x,\frac{r}{3})} \frac{2^{a^3}}{V(x,y)} \,d\mu(y) \\ &\le 2^{a^3+6a} \int_{B(x,3r) \setminus B(x,\frac{r}{3})} \frac{1}{\mu(B(x,\frac{r}{3}))} \,d\mu(y) \\ &\le 2^{a^3+6a} \frac{\mu(B(x,3r))}{\mu(B(x,\frac{r}{3}))} \\ &\le 2^{a^3+10a}.
nodes.label: eq-J2-diff-est-4

nodes.name: Combine the estimates and use the choice of c
nodes.statement_short: Combine the estimates and use the choice of c

nodes.name: Estimate F set
nodes.statement_short: Weak-type bound for the auxiliary function $F$ outside $\Omega$.
nodes.statement: For $F$ as defined in \Cref{estimate-bad-partial}, we have \begin{equation} \mu(\{x\in X\setminus\Omega: F(x)>\alpha/8\}) \le \frac{2^{a^3+11a+4}}{\alpha} \int |f(y)|\,d\mu(y)\,. \end{equation}
nodes.label: estimate-F-set

nodes.name: Measure bound for {F > alpha/8} off Omega
nodes.statement: \mu(\{x\in X\setminus\Omega: F(x)>\alpha/8\}) \le \frac{2^{a^3+11a+4}}{\alpha} \int |f(y)|\,d\mu(y)\,.
nodes.label: eq-F-X-minus-Omega

nodes.name: Proof of Estimate F set
nodes.statement_short: Chebyshev, then dyadic annuli around $x_j$ and a geometric series bound each term; sum with the ball-measure bound.
nodes.statement: We estimate \begin{align} \mu(\{x\in X\setminus\Omega&: F(x)> \alpha/8\}) \le \frac{8}{\alpha} \int_{X\setminus \Omega} F(x)\,d\mu(x) \\ &\le \frac{8}{\alpha} \int_{X\setminus \Omega} 2^{a^3+2a+1} c\alpha \sum_{j} \left(\frac{3r_j}{\rho(x,x_j)}\right)^{\frac{1}{a}}\frac{\mu(B_{3,j})}{V(x,x_j)}\,d\mu(x) \\ &\le 2^{a^3+2a+4} c \sum_{j} \mu(B_{3,j}) \int_{X\setminus B_{6,j}} \left(\frac{3r_j}{\rho(x,x_j)}\right)^{\frac{1}{a}}\frac{1}{V(x,x_j)}\,d\mu(x) \end{align} Using \begin{equation*} V(x,x_j) = \mu(B(x,\rho(x,x_j))) \ge 2^{-a}\mu(B(x,2\rho(x,x_j))) \ge 2^{-a} \mu(B(x_j,\rho(x_j,x))), \end{equation*} we have for all $j\in J$, \begin{align*} &\int_{X\setminus B_{6,j}} \left(\frac{3r_j}{\rho(x,x_j)}\right)^{\frac{1}{a}}\frac{1}{V(x,x_j)}\,d\mu(x) \\ \le& 2^a \int_{X\setminus B_{6,j}} \left(\frac{3r_j}{\rho(x,x_j)}\right)^{\frac{1}{a}}\frac{1}{\mu(B(x_j,\rho(x_j,x)))}\,d\mu(x) \\ \le&2^a \sum_{n=1}^\infty \int_{B(x_j,2^{n+1}\cdot3r_j)\setminus B(x_j,2^n\cdot3r_j)} \left(\frac{3r_j}{2^n \cdot3r_j}\right)^{\frac{1}{a}}\frac{1}{\mu(B(x_j,2^n \cdot3r_j))}\,d\mu(x) \\ \le&2^a \sum_{n=1}^\infty 2^{-\frac{n}{a}} \frac{\mu(B(x_j,2^{n+1}\cdot3r_j))}{\mu(B(x_j,2^n \cdot3r_j))} \\ \le&2^{3a}, \end{align*} where we used \Cref{geometric-series-estimate} in the last step. Plugging this into \eqref{eq-F-est-1} and using \eqref{eq-bset-length-sum}, we conclude that \begin{equation*} \mu(\{x\in X\setminus\Omega: F(x)> \alpha/8\}) \le \frac{2^{a^3+11a+4}}{\alpha} \int |f(y)|\,d\mu(y)\,. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Chebyshev and insertion of the definition of F
nodes.statement_short: Chebyshev and insertion of the definition of F

nodes.name: Chebyshev bound for F
nodes.statement: \mu(\{x\in X\setminus\Omega&: F(x)> \alpha/8\}) \le \frac{8}{\alpha} \int_{X\setminus \Omega} F(x)\,d\mu(x) \\ &\le \frac{8}{\alpha} \int_{X\setminus \Omega} 2^{a^3+2a+1} c\alpha \sum_{j} \left(\frac{3r_j}{\rho(x,x_j)}\right)^{\frac{1}{a}}\frac{\mu(B_{3,j})}{V(x,x_j)}\,d\mu(x) \\ &\le 2^{a^3+2a+4} c \sum_{j} \mu(B_{3,j}) \int_{X\setminus B_{6,j}} \left(\frac{3r_j}{\rho(x,x_j)}\right)^{\frac{1}{a}}\frac{1}{V(x,x_j)}\,d\mu(x)
nodes.label: eq-F-est-1

nodes.name: Bound each annular integral by a geometric series
nodes.statement_short: Bound each annular integral by a geometric series

nodes.name: Plug in and use the total ball measure bound
nodes.statement_short: Plug in and use the total ball measure bound

nodes.name: Estimate bad
nodes.statement_short: Weak-type bound for $T_r b$ on the bad part.
nodes.statement: We have \begin{equation*} \mu\left({\{x\in X: |T_r b(x)|>\alpha/2\}}\right) \le \frac{\frac{2^{7a}}{c} + 2^{a^3+11a+4}}{\alpha} \int |f(y)|\,d\mu(y) \,. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: estimate-bad

nodes.name: Proof of Estimate bad
nodes.statement_short: Split off $\Omega$, bound $\mu(\Omega)$ by the ball measures, and reduce the rest to the $F$-set estimate.
nodes.statement: We estimate \begin{equation*} \mu\left(\{x\in X: |T_r b(x)|>\alpha/2\}\right) \end{equation*} \begin{equation} \le \mu (\Omega) + \mu\left(\{x\in X\setminus\Omega: |T_r b(x)|>{\alpha}/2\}\right)\,. \end{equation} Using \eqref{eq-Ij*-dim} and \eqref{eq-bset-length-sum}, we conclude that \begin{equation} \mu(\Omega) \le \sum_{j} \mu (B_{6,j}) \le 2^a \sum_j \mu(B_{3,j}) \le \frac{2^{7a}}{c\alpha} \int |f(y)|\, d\mu(y)\,. \end{equation} It follows from \Cref{estimate-bad-partial} and the triangle inequality that \begin{equation} \mu({\{x\in X\setminus\Omega: |T_r b(x)|>\alpha/2\}}) \le \mu(\{x\in X\setminus\Omega: F(x)> \alpha/8\})\,. \end{equation} The claim now follows from \Cref{estimate-F-set}.

nodes.name: Split the level set into Omega and its complement
nodes.statement_short: Split the level set into Omega and its complement

nodes.name: Split off Omega
nodes.statement: \le \mu (\Omega) + \mu\left(\{x\in X\setminus\Omega: |T_r b(x)|>{\alpha}/2\}\right)\,.
nodes.label: eq-set-dec-2

nodes.name: Bound the measure of Omega
nodes.statement:
Using \eqref{eq-Ij*-dim} and \eqref{eq-bset-length-sum}, we conclude that
    \begin{equation} \mu(\Omega) \le \sum_{j} \mu (B_{6,j})
        \le 2^a \sum_j \mu(B_{3,j}) \le \frac{2^{7a}}{c\alpha} \int |f(y)|\, d\mu(y)\,.
    \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the measure of Omega

nodes.name: Measure bound for Omega
nodes.statement: \mu(\Omega) \le \sum_{j} \mu (B_{6,j}) \le 2^a \sum_j \mu(B_{3,j}) \le \frac{2^{7a}}{c\alpha} \int |f(y)|\, d\mu(y)\,.
nodes.label: eq-omega-bd

nodes.name: Reduce to the F set by Estimate bad partial
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the F set by Estimate bad partial

nodes.name: Reduction to the F set
nodes.statement: \mu({\{x\in X\setminus\Omega: |T_r b(x)|>\alpha/2\}}) \le \mu(\{x\in X\setminus\Omega: F(x)> \alpha/8\})\,.
nodes.label: eq-set-dec-3

nodes.name: Conclude by Estimate F set
nodes.statement: The claim now follows from \Cref{estimate-F-set}.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by Estimate F set

nodes.name: Proof of the Calderon-Zygmund weak (1,1) theorem
nodes.statement_short: Split $T_r f=T_r g+T_r b$, apply Estimate good and Estimate bad, and insert the choice of $c$.
nodes.statement: It follows by the triangle inequality and subadditivity of $\mu$ that \begin{equation*} \mu\left(\{x\in X: |T_r f(x)|>\alpha\}\right) \end{equation*} \begin{equation*} \le \mu\left(\{x\in X: |T_r g(x)|>{\alpha}/2\}\right) + \mu\left(\{x\in X: |T_r b(x)|>{\alpha}/2\}\right). \end{equation*} Using \Cref{estimate-good}, \Cref{estimate-bad} and the definition \eqref{weak-1-1-proof-cz-const} of $c$, we get \begin{align*} \le& \frac{2^{2a^3+3a+2}c + \frac{2^{7a}}{c} + 2^{a^3+11a+4}}{\alpha} \int |f(y)|\, d\mu(y) \\ =& \frac{2^{a^3-9a-2} + 2^{a^3+19a+4} + 2^{a^3+11a+4}}{\alpha} \int |f(y)|\, d\mu(y) \\ \le& \frac{2^{a^3 + 21a}}{\alpha} \int |f(y)|\, d\mu(y). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Splitting the level set of T_r f
nodes.statement: \le \mu\left(\{x\in X: |T_r g(x)|>{\alpha}/2\}\right) + \mu\left(\{x\in X: |T_r b(x)|>{\alpha}/2\}\right).
nodes.label: eq-set-dec-1

nodes.name: Fixed function $f$ and tolerance $\epsilon$
nodes.statement: Let a uniformly continuous $2\pi$-periodic function $f:{\mathbb{R}}\to \mathbb{C}$ and $\epsilon>0$ be given.

nodes.name: Constant $C_{a,q}$
nodes.statement_short: $C_{a,q}=2^{474a^3}/(q-1)^6$, the constant of the two-sided metric space Carleson theorem.

nodes.name: Auxiliary tolerance $\epsilon'$ and constant $C_\epsilon$
nodes.statement_short: $\epsilon'=\epsilon/(4C_\epsilon)$ with $C_\epsilon=(8/(\pi\epsilon))^{1/2}C_{4,2}+\pi$.

nodes.name: Definition of $\epsilon'$
nodes.statement: \epsilon' := \frac {\epsilon} {4 C_\epsilon} \,,

nodes.name: Uniform continuity of $f$
nodes.statement: Since $f$ is continuous and periodic, $f$ is uniformly continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Continuous periodic functions are uniformly continuous.

nodes.name: Existence of the modulus $\delta$
nodes.statement:
Thus, there is a $0<\delta<\pi$
such that for all $x,x' \in {\mathbb{R}}$ with $|x-x'|\le \delta$
we have
\begin{equation} |f(x)-f(x')|\le \epsilon' \, .
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Uniform continuity gives $\delta\in(0,\pi)$ with $|f(x)-f(x')|\le\epsilon'$ whenever $|x-x'|\le\delta$.

nodes.name: Uniform continuity bound
nodes.statement: |f(x)-f(x')|\le \epsilon' \, .
nodes.label: uniconbound

nodes.name: Smoothed function $f_0$
nodes.statement:
Define
\begin{equation} f_0:=f \ast \phi_\delta,
\end{equation}
where $\phi_\delta$ is a nonnegative smooth bump function with $\operatorname{supp} (\phi_\delta) \subset (-\delta, \delta)$ and $\int _{\mathbb{R}} \phi_\delta (x) \, dx = 1$.
differentia: $\phi_\delta$ is a nonnegative smooth bump function with $\operatorname{supp} (\phi_\delta) \subset (-\delta, \delta)$ and $\int _{\mathbb{R}} \phi_\delta (x) \, dx = 1$
nodes.statement_short: $f_0=f*\phi_\delta$ with $\phi_\delta$ a smooth unit-mass bump supported in $(-\delta,\delta)$.

nodes.name: Definition of $f_0$
nodes.statement: f_0:=f \ast \phi_\delta,
nodes.label: def-fzero

nodes.name: smooth approximation
assumptions: Let a uniformly continuous $2\pi$-periodic function $f:{\mathbb{R}}\to \mathbb{C}$ and $\epsilon>0$ be given.
conclusions: The function $f_0$ is smooth (and therefore measurable).
nodes.statement_short: The mollified $f_0$ is periodic, smooth and uniformly $\epsilon'$-close to $f$.
nodes.statement: The function $f_0$ is $2\pi$-periodic. The function $f_0$ is smooth (and therefore measurable). The function $f_0$ satisfies for all $x\in {\mathbb{R}}$: \begin{equation} |f(x)-f_0(x)|\le \epsilon' \, , \end{equation}
nodes.label: smooth-approximation

nodes.name: $f_0$ close to $f$
nodes.statement: |f(x)-f_0(x)|\le \epsilon' \, ,
nodes.label: eq-ffzero

nodes.name: Proof of smooth approximation
nodes.statement_short: Periodicity from the definition; smoothness and the approximation bound are in the Lean library.
nodes.statement: Periodicity follows directly from the definitions. The other properties are part of the Lean library.

nodes.name: convergence for smooth
nodes.statement_short: Partial Fourier sums of $f_0$ converge uniformly: eventually within $\epsilon/4$.
nodes.statement: There exists some $N_0 \in {\mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $N>N_0$ and $x\in [0,2\pi]$ we have \begin{equation} |S_N f_0 (x)- f_0(x)|\le \frac \epsilon 4\, . \end{equation}
nodes.label: convergence-for-smooth

nodes.name: Uniform convergence bound for $f_0$
nodes.statement: |S_N f_0 (x)- f_0(x)|\le \frac \epsilon 4\, .

nodes.name: control approximation effect
conclusions: There is a set $E \subset {\mathbb{R}}$ with Lebesgue measure $|E|\le \epsilon$
nodes.statement_short: Outside an exceptional set of measure $\le\epsilon$, all partial sums of $f-f_0$ are at most $\epsilon/4$.
nodes.statement: There is a set $E \subset {\mathbb{R}}$ with Lebesgue measure $|E|\le \epsilon$ such that for all \begin{equation} x\in [0,2\pi)\setminus E \end{equation} we have \begin{equation} \sup_{N\ge 0} |S_Nf(x)-S_Nf_0(x)| \le \frac \epsilon 4\,. \end{equation}
nodes.label: control-approximation-effect

nodes.name: Points outside $E$
nodes.statement: x\in [0,2\pi)\setminus E

nodes.name: Maximal partial sum difference bound
nodes.statement: \sup_{N\ge 0} |S_Nf(x)-S_Nf_0(x)| \le \frac \epsilon 4\,.
nodes.label: eq-max-partial-sum-diff

nodes.name: classical Carleson with exceptional sets
assumptions: Let $f$ be a $2\pi$-periodic complex-valued continuous function on $\mathbb{R}$.
conclusions: there exists a Borel set $E\subset [0,2\pi]$ with Lebesgue measure $|E|\le \epsilon$ and a positive integer $N_0$
nodes.statement_short: For continuous periodic $f$ and $\epsilon>0$, $S_Nf$ is uniformly $\epsilon$-close to $f$ for large $N$ outside a set of measure $\le\epsilon$.
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a $2\pi$-periodic complex-valued continuous function on $\mathbb{R}$. For all $\epsilon>0$, there exists a Borel set $E\subset [0,2\pi]$ with Lebesgue measure $|E|\le \epsilon$ and a positive integer $N_0$ such that for all $x\in [0,2\pi]\setminus E$ and all integers $N>N_0$, we have \begin{equation} |f(x)-S_N f(x)|\le \epsilon. \end{equation}
nodes.label: exceptional-set-carleson

nodes.name: Approximation bound for $S_Nf$
nodes.statement: |f(x)-S_N f(x)|\le \epsilon.
nodes.label: aeconv

nodes.name: Proof of classical Carleson with exceptional sets
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality splitting $f-S_Nf$ via $f_0$, then bound each term by the three preceding lemmas.
nodes.statement: Let $N_0$ be as in \Cref{convergence-for-smooth}. For every \begin{equation} x\in [0, 2\pi) \setminus E\, , \end{equation} and every $N>N_0$ we have by the triangle inequality \begin{equation*} |f(x)-S_Nf(x)| \end{equation*} \begin{equation} \le |f(x)-f_0(x)|+ |f_0(x)-S_Nf_0(x)|+|S_Nf_0(x)-S_N f(x)|\, . \end{equation} Using \Cref{smooth-approximation,convergence-for-smooth,control-approximation-effect}, we estimate \eqref{epsilonthird} by \begin{equation} \le \epsilon' +\frac \epsilon 4 +\frac \epsilon 4\le \epsilon\, . \end{equation} This shows \eqref{aeconv} for the given $E$ and $N_0$.

nodes.name: Fix $N_0$ and split $f-S_Nf$ by the triangle inequality through $f_0$
nodes.statement_short: Fix $N_0$ and split $f-S_Nf$ by the triangle inequality through $f_0$

nodes.name: Points outside $E$ (proof)
nodes.statement: x\in [0, 2\pi) \setminus E\, ,

nodes.name: Bound the three terms by the three lemmas
nodes.statement_short: Bound the three terms by the three lemmas

nodes.name: Final estimate by $\epsilon$
nodes.statement: \le \epsilon' +\frac \epsilon 4 +\frac \epsilon 4\le \epsilon\, .

nodes.name: Conclude the approximation bound
nodes.statement: This shows \eqref{aeconv} for the given $E$ and $N_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the approximation bound

nodes.name: Proof of the classical Carleson theorem
nodes.statement_short: Apply the exceptional-set version with $\epsilon_n=2^{-n}\delta$, take unions, then intersect over $\delta\to0$.
nodes.statement: By applying \Cref{exceptional-set-carleson} with a sequence of $\epsilon_n:= 2^{-n}\delta$ for $n\ge 1$ and taking the union of corresponding exceptional sets $E_n$, we see that outside a set of measure $\delta$, the partial Fourier sums converge pointwise for $N\to \infty$. Applying this with a sequence of $\delta$ shrinking to zero and taking the intersection of the corresponding exceptional sets, which has measure zero, we see that the Fourier series converges outside a set of measure zero.

nodes.name: Hilbert kernel $\kappa$
nodes.statement:
Let $\kappa:{\mathbb{R}}\to \mathbb{C}$ be the function defined by
$\kappa(0)=0$ and for $0<|x|<1$
\begin{equation} \kappa(x)=\frac { 1-|x|}{1-e^{ix}}\,
\end{equation}
and for $|x|\ge 1$,
\begin{equation} \kappa(x)=0\, .
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\kappa(x)=(1-|x|)/(1-e^{ix})$ for $0<|x|<1$ and $0$ otherwise (truncated Hilbert kernel).

nodes.name: Hilbert kernel on $0<|x|<1$
nodes.statement: \kappa(x)=\frac { 1-|x|}{1-e^{ix}}\,
nodes.label: eq-hilker

nodes.name: Hilbert kernel vanishes for $|x|\ge1$
nodes.statement: \kappa(x)=0\, .
nodes.label: eq-hilker1

nodes.name: Continuity of $\kappa$ away from $0$
nodes.statement: Note that this function is continuous at every point $x$ with $|x|>0$.

nodes.name: real Carleson
assumptions: Let $F,G$ be Borel subsets of ${\mathbb{R}}$ with finite measure.
Let $f$ be a bounded measurable function on ${\mathbb{R}}$ with $|f|\le \mathbf{1}_F$.
nodes.statement_short: Restricted weak-type $(2,2)$ bound for the real-line Carleson maximal operator $T$ with constant $C_{4,2}$.
nodes.statement: Let $F,G$ be Borel subsets of ${\mathbb{R}}$ with finite measure. Let $f$ be a bounded measurable function on ${\mathbb{R}}$ with $|f|\le \mathbf{1}_F$. Then \begin{equation} \left|\int _G Tf(x) \, dx\right| \le C_{4,2} |F|^{\frac 12} |G|^{\frac 12} \, , \end{equation} where \begin{equation} T f(x)=\sup_{n\in \mathbb{Z}} \sup_{r>0}\left|\int_{r<|x-y|<1} f(y)\kappa(x-y) e^{iny}\, dy\right|\, . \end{equation}
nodes.label: real-Carleson

nodes.name: Restricted weak type bound for $T$
nodes.statement: \left|\int _G Tf(x) \, dx\right| \le C_{4,2} |F|^{\frac 12} |G|^{\frac 12} \, ,

nodes.name: Real Carleson maximal operator $T$
nodes.statement: T f(x)=\sup_{n\in \mathbb{Z}} \sup_{r>0}\left|\int_{r<|x-y|<1} f(y)\kappa(x-y) e^{iny}\, dy\right|\, .
nodes.label: define-T-carleson

nodes.name: Hilbert strong 2 2
assumptions: Let $f$ be a bounded, measurable function on $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: The truncated Hilbert transform $H_r$ is bounded on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ with norm $\le 2^9$, uniformly in $r$.
nodes.statement: Let $0<r$. Let $f$ be a bounded, measurable function on $\mathbb{R}$. Then \begin{equation} \|H_rf\|_{2}\leq 2^{9} \|f\|_2, \end{equation} where \begin{equation} H_r f(x) := T_r f(x) = \int_{r\le |x-y|} \kappa(x-y) f(y) \, dy \end{equation}
nodes.label: Hilbert-strong-2-2

nodes.name: Truncated Hilbert transform $H_r$
nodes.statement: H_r f(x) := T_r f(x) = \int_{r\le |x-y|} \kappa(x-y) f(y) \, dy
nodes.label: def-H-r

nodes.name: van der Corput
nodes.statement_short: Oscillatory integral of a Lipschitz $g$ against $e^{inx}$ decays like $(1+|n||\beta-\alpha|)^{-1}$.
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha\le\beta$ be real numbers. Let $g:{\mathbb{R}}\to \mathbb{C}$ be a measurable function and assume \begin{equation} \|g\|_{Lip(\alpha,\beta)}:=\sup_{\alpha\le x\le \beta}|g(x)|+\frac{|\beta-\alpha|}{2} \sup_{\alpha\le x<y\le \beta} \frac {|g(y)-g(x)|}{|y-x|}<\infty\, . \end{equation} Then for any $\alpha \le \beta$ and $n\in{\mathbb{Z}}$ we have \begin{equation} \int _{\alpha}^{\beta} g(x) e^{inx}\, dx\le 2\pi |\beta-\alpha|\|g\|_{Lip(\alpha,\beta)}(1+|n||\beta-\alpha|)^{-1}\, . \end{equation}
nodes.label: van-der-Corput

nodes.name: Lipschitz norm on $[\alpha,\beta]$
nodes.statement: \|g\|_{Lip(\alpha,\beta)}:=\sup_{\alpha\le x\le \beta}|g(x)|+\frac{|\beta-\alpha|}{2} \sup_{\alpha\le x<y\le \beta} \frac {|g(y)-g(x)|}{|y-x|}<\infty\, .

nodes.name: van der Corput bound
nodes.statement: \int _{\alpha}^{\beta} g(x) e^{inx}\, dx\le 2\pi |\beta-\alpha|\|g\|_{Lip(\alpha,\beta)}(1+|n||\beta-\alpha|)^{-1}\, .

nodes.name: Dirichlet kernel
nodes.statement_short: $S_Nf$ is convolution with the Dirichlet kernel $K_N$, which has the closed form $e^{iNx}/(1-e^{-ix})+e^{-iNx}/(1-e^{ix})$.
nodes.statement: We have for every $2\pi$-periodic bounded measurable $f$ and every $N\ge 0$ \begin{equation} S_Nf(x)=\frac 1{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}f(y) K_N(x-y)\, dy \end{equation} where $K_N$ is the $2\pi$-periodic continuous function of ${\mathbb{R}}$ given by \begin{equation} \sum_{n=-N}^N e^{in x'}\, . \end{equation} We have for $e^{ix'}\neq 1$ that \begin{equation} K_N(x')=\frac{e^{iNx'}}{1-e^{-ix'}} +\frac {e^{-iNx'}}{1-e^{ix'}} \, . \end{equation}
nodes.label: Dirichlet-kernel

nodes.name: Partial sum as convolution with $K_N$
nodes.statement: S_Nf(x)=\frac 1{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}f(y) K_N(x-y)\, dy

nodes.name: Dirichlet kernel as exponential sum
nodes.statement: \sum_{n=-N}^N e^{in x'}\, .
nodes.label: eqksumexp

nodes.name: Closed form of the Dirichlet kernel
nodes.label: eqksumhil

nodes.name: Proof of Dirichlet kernel
nodes.statement_short: Interchange sum and integral; then a telescoping identity gives the closed form.
nodes.statement: We have by definitions and interchanging sum and integral \begin{equation*} S_Nf(x)=\sum_{n=-N}^N \widehat{f}_n e^{inx} \end{equation*} \begin{equation*} =\sum_{n=-N}^N \frac 1{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi} f(x) e^{in(x-y)}\, dy \end{equation*} \begin{equation} =\frac 1{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi} f(y) \sum_{n=-N}^N e^{in(x-y)}\, dy\, . \end{equation} This proves the first statement of the lemma. By a telescoping sum, we have for every $x'\in {\mathbb{R}}$ \begin{equation} \left( e^{\frac 12 ix'}-e^{-\frac 12 ix'}\right) \sum_{n=-N}^N e^{inx'}= e^{(N+\frac 12) ix'}-e^{-(N+\frac 12) ix'}\, . \end{equation} If $e^{ix'}\neq 1$, the first factor on the left-hand side is not $0$ and we may divide by this factor to obtain \begin{equation} \sum_{n=-N}^N e^{inx'}= \frac{e^{i(N+\frac 1 2)x'}}{e^{\frac 12 ix'}-e^{-\frac 12ix'}} -\frac{e^{-i(N+\frac 1 2)x'}}{e^{\frac 12 ix'}-e^{-\frac 12ix'}} =\frac{e^{iNx'}}{1-e^{-ix'}} +\frac {e^{-iNx'}}{1-e^{ix'}}\, . \end{equation} This proves the second part of the lemma.

nodes.name: Interchange sum and integral to get the convolution formula
nodes.statement_short: Interchange sum and integral to get the convolution formula

nodes.name: Convolution form of $S_Nf$
nodes.statement: =\frac 1{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi} f(y) \sum_{n=-N}^N e^{in(x-y)}\, dy\, .
nodes.label: eq-expsum

nodes.name: Telescoping identity for the exponential sum
nodes.statement_short: Telescoping identity for the exponential sum

nodes.name: Telescoping identity
nodes.statement: \left( e^{\frac 12 ix'}-e^{-\frac 12 ix'}\right) \sum_{n=-N}^N e^{inx'}= e^{(N+\frac 12) ix'}-e^{-(N+\frac 12) ix'}\, .

nodes.name: Divide by the nonzero factor to get the closed form
nodes.statement_short: Divide by the nonzero factor to get the closed form

nodes.name: Closed form of the exponential sum
nodes.statement: \sum_{n=-N}^N e^{inx'}= \frac{e^{i(N+\frac 1 2)x'}}{e^{\frac 12 ix'}-e^{-\frac 12ix'}} -\frac{e^{-i(N+\frac 1 2)x'}}{e^{\frac 12 ix'}-e^{-\frac 12ix'}} =\frac{e^{iNx'}}{1-e^{-ix'}} +\frac {e^{-iNx'}}{1-e^{ix'}}\, .

nodes.name: lower secant bound
nodes.statement_short: $|1-e^{ix}|\ge 2\eta/\pi$ when $x$ stays $\eta$-away from multiples of $2\pi$.
nodes.statement: Let $\eta>0$ and $-2\pi +\eta \le x\le 2\pi-\eta$ with $|x|\ge \eta$. Then \begin{equation} |1-e^{ix}|\ge \frac{2}{\pi} \eta \end{equation}
nodes.label: lower-secant-bound

nodes.name: Lower secant bound
nodes.statement: |1-e^{ix}|\ge \frac{2}{\pi} \eta

nodes.name: Proof of lower secant bound
nodes.statement_short: Bound by $|\sin x|$ and use concavity of $\sin$ on each quarter period.
nodes.statement: We have $$ |1 - e^{ix}| = \sqrt{(1 - \cos(x))^2 + \sin^2(x)} \ge |\sin(x)|\,. $$ If $0 \le x \le \frac{\pi}{2}$, then we have from concavity of $\sin$ on $[0, \pi]$ and $\sin(0) = 0$ and $\sin(\frac{\pi}{2}) = 1$ $$ |\sin(x)| \ge \frac{2}{\pi} x \ge \frac{2}{\pi} \eta\,. $$ When $x\in \frac{m\pi}{2} + [0, \frac{\pi}{2}]$ for $m \in \{-4, -3, -2, -1, 1, 2, 3\}$ one can argue similarly.

nodes.name: Bound $|1-e^{ix}|$ below by $|\sin x|$
nodes.statement:
We have
    $$
        |1 - e^{ix}| = \sqrt{(1 - \cos(x))^2 + \sin^2(x)} \ge |\sin(x)|\,.
    $$
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|1-e^{ix}|$ below by $|\sin x|$

nodes.name: Concavity of $\sin$ on $[0,\pi/2]$; other quarter periods similarly
nodes.statement:
If $0 \le x \le \frac{\pi}{2}$, then we have from concavity of $\sin$ on $[0, \pi]$ and $\sin(0) = 0$ and $\sin(\frac{\pi}{2}) = 1$
    $$
        |\sin(x)| \ge \frac{2}{\pi} x \ge \frac{2}{\pi} \eta\,.
    $$
    When $x\in \frac{m\pi}{2} + [0, \frac{\pi}{2}]$ for $m \in \{-4, -3, -2, -1, 1, 2, 3\}$ one can argue similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Concavity of $\sin$ on $[0,\pi/2]$; other quarter periods similarly

nodes.name: spectral projection bound
assumptions: Let $f$ be a bounded $2\pi$-periodic measurable function.
nodes.statement_short: Partial Fourier sums are $L^2$ contractions.
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a bounded $2\pi$-periodic measurable function. Then, for all $N\ge 0$ \begin{equation} \|S_Nf\|_{L^2[0, 2\pi]} \le \|f\|_{L^2[0, 2\pi]}. \end{equation}
nodes.label: spectral-projection-bound

nodes.name: Hilbert kernel bound
nodes.statement_short: Size bound $|\kappa(x-y)|\lesssim |x-y|^{-1}$ for the Hilbert kernel.
nodes.statement: For $x,y\in {\mathbb{R}}$ with $x\neq y$ we have \begin{equation} |\kappa(x-y)|\le 2^2(2|x-y|)^{-1}\, . \end{equation}
nodes.label: Hilbert-kernel-bound

nodes.name: Proof of Hilbert kernel bound
nodes.statement_short: Trivial if $\kappa=0$; otherwise $|x-y|<1$ and the lower secant bound gives $2/|x-y|$.
nodes.statement: Fix $x\neq y$. If $\kappa(x-y)$ is zero, then \eqref{eqcarl30} is evident. Assume $\kappa(x-y)$ is not zero, then $0<|x-y|<1$. We have \begin{equation} |\kappa(x-y)|=\left|\frac {1-|x-y|}{1-e^{i(x-y)}}\right|\, . \end{equation} We estimate with \Cref{lower-secant-bound} \begin{equation} |\kappa(x-y)|\le \frac {1}{|1-e^{i(x-y)}|}\le \frac 2{|x-y|}\, . \end{equation} This proves \eqref{eqcarl30} in the given case and completes the proof of the lemma.

nodes.name: Case $\kappa(x-y)=0$ is evident
nodes.statement: Fix $x\neq y$. If $\kappa(x-y)$ is zero, then \eqref{eqcarl30} is evident.
nodes.statement_short: Case $\kappa(x-y)=0$ is evident

nodes.name: Case $\kappa(x-y)\ne0$: write out and bound by the lower secant bound
nodes.statement_short: Case $\kappa(x-y)\ne0$: write out and bound by the lower secant bound

nodes.name: Then $0<|x-y|<1$ and write out $\kappa$
nodes.statement:
Assume $\kappa(x-y)$ is not zero, then $0<|x-y|<1$.
    We have
\begin{equation} |\kappa(x-y)|=\left|\frac {1-|x-y|}{1-e^{i(x-y)}}\right|\, .
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Then $0<|x-y|<1$ and write out $\kappa$

nodes.name: Formula for $|\kappa(x-y)|$
nodes.statement: |\kappa(x-y)|=\left|\frac {1-|x-y|}{1-e^{i(x-y)}}\right|\, .
nodes.label: eqcarl31

nodes.name: Apply the lower secant bound and conclude
nodes.statement_short: Apply the lower secant bound and conclude

nodes.name: Secant estimate of $|\kappa(x-y)|$
nodes.statement: |\kappa(x-y)|\le \frac {1}{|1-e^{i(x-y)}|}\le \frac 2{|x-y|}\, .
nodes.label: eqcarl311

nodes.name: Hilbert kernel regularity
nodes.statement_short: Hölder-type smoothness estimate for the Hilbert kernel $\kappa$.
nodes.statement: For $x,y,y'\in {\mathbb{R}}$ with $x\neq y,y'$ and \begin{equation} 2|y-y'|\le |x-y|\, , \end{equation} we have \begin{equation} |\kappa(x-y) - \kappa(x-y')|\le 2^{8}\frac{1}{|x-y|} \frac{|y-y'|}{|x-y|}\, . \end{equation}
nodes.label: Hilbert-kernel-regularity

nodes.name: Hilbert kernel regularity bound
nodes.statement: |\kappa(x-y) - \kappa(x-y')|\le 2^{8}\frac{1}{|x-y|} \frac{|y-y'|}{|x-y|}\, .
nodes.label: eqcarl301

nodes.name: Proof of Hilbert kernel regularity
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $x=0$, $y,y'>0$; split into four cases by $y,y'\lessgtr 1$. The main case uses the fundamental theorem of calculus with the lower secant bound.
nodes.statement: Upon replacing $y$ by $y-x$ and $y'$ by $y'-x$ on the left-hand side of \eqref{eq-close-hoelder}, we can assume that $x = 0$. Then the assumption \eqref{eq-close-hoelder} implies that $y$ and $y'$ have the same sign. Since $\kappa(y) = \bar \kappa(-y)$ we can assume that they are both positive. Then it follows from \eqref{eq-close-hoelder} that $$ \frac{y}{2} \le y' \,. $$ We distinguish four cases. If $y, y' \le 1$, then we have $$ |\kappa(-y) - \kappa(-y')| = \left| \frac{1 - y}{1- e^{-iy}} - \frac{1 - y'}{1- e^{-iy'}}\right| $$ and by the fundamental theorem of calculus $$ = \left| \int_{y'}^{y} \frac{-1 + e^{-it} + i(1-t)e^{it}}{(1 - e^{-it})^2} \,dt \right|\,. $$ Using $y' \ge \frac{y}{2}$ and \Cref{lower-secant-bound}, we bound this by $$ \le |y - y'| \sup_{\frac{y}{2} \le t \le 1} \frac{3}{|1 - e^{-it}|^2} \le 3 |y-y'| (2 \frac{2}{y})^2 \le 2^{6} \frac{|y-y'|}{|y|^2}\,. $$ If $y \le 1$ and $y' > 1$, then $\kappa(-y') = 0$ and we have from the first case $$ |\kappa(-y) - \kappa(-y')| = |\kappa(-y) - \kappa(-1)| \le 2^{6} \frac{|y-1|}{|y|^2} \le 2^{6} \frac{|y-y'|}{|y|^2}\,. $$ Similarly, if $y > 1$ and $y' \le 1$, then $\kappa(-y) = 0$ and we have from the first case $$ |\kappa(-y) - \kappa(-y')| = |\kappa(-y') - \kappa(-1)| \le 2^{6} \frac{|y'-1|}{|y'|^2} \le 2^{6} \frac{|y-y'|}{|y'|^2}\,. $$ Using again $y' \ge \frac{y}{2}$, we bound this by $$ \le 2^{6} \frac{|y-y'|}{|y / 2|^2} = 2^{8} \frac{|y-y'|}{|y|^2} $$ Finally, if $y, y' > 1$ then $$ |\kappa(-y) - \kappa(-y')| = 0 \le 2^{8} \frac{|y-y'|}{|y|^2}\,. $$

nodes.name: Reduce to $x=0$ and $y,y'$ positive
nodes.statement: Upon replacing $y$ by $y-x$ and $y'$ by $y'-x$ on the left-hand side of \eqref{eq-close-hoelder}, we can assume that $x = 0$. Then the assumption \eqref{eq-close-hoelder} implies that $y$ and $y'$ have the same sign. Since $\kappa(y) = \bar \kappa(-y)$ we can assume that they are both positive.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $x=0$ and $y,y'$ positive

nodes.name: Deduce $y/2\le y'$
nodes.statement:
Then it follows from \eqref{eq-close-hoelder} that

        \frac{y}{2} \le y' \,.

nodes.name: Case $y,y'\le1$: fundamental theorem of calculus and lower secant bound
nodes.statement:
We distinguish four cases. If $y, y' \le 1$, then we have
    $$
        |\kappa(-y) - \kappa(-y')| = \left| \frac{1 - y}{1- e^{-iy}} - \frac{1 - y'}{1- e^{-iy'}}\right|
    $$
    and by the fundamental theorem of calculus
    $$
        = \left| \int_{y'}^{y} \frac{-1 + e^{-it} + i(1-t)e^{it}}{(1 - e^{-it})^2} \,dt \right|\,.
    $$
    Using $y' \ge \frac{y}{2}$ and \Cref{lower-secant-bound}, we bound this by
    $$
        \le |y - y'| \sup_{\frac{y}{2} \le t \le 1} \frac{3}{|1 - e^{-it}|^2} \le 3 |y-y'| (2 \frac{2}{y})^2 \le 2^{6} \frac{|y-y'|}{|y|^2}\,.
    $$
nodes.statement_short: Case $y,y'\le1$: fundamental theorem of calculus and lower secant bound

nodes.name: Case $y\le1<y'$: reduce to the first case
nodes.statement:
If $y \le 1$ and $y' > 1$, then $\kappa(-y') = 0$ and we have from the first case
    $$
        |\kappa(-y) - \kappa(-y')| = |\kappa(-y) - \kappa(-1)| \le 2^{6} \frac{|y-1|}{|y|^2} \le 2^{6} \frac{|y-y'|}{|y|^2}\,.
    $$
nodes.statement_short: Case $y\le1<y'$: reduce to the first case

nodes.name: Case $y'\le1<y$: reduce to the first case and use $y'\ge y/2$
nodes.statement:
Similarly, if $y > 1$ and $y' \le 1$, then $\kappa(-y) = 0$ and we have from the first case
    $$
        |\kappa(-y) - \kappa(-y')| = |\kappa(-y') - \kappa(-1)| \le 2^{6} \frac{|y'-1|}{|y'|^2} \le 2^{6} \frac{|y-y'|}{|y'|^2}\,.
    $$
    Using again $y' \ge \frac{y}{2}$, we bound this by
    $$
        \le 2^{6} \frac{|y-y'|}{|y / 2|^2} = 2^{8} \frac{|y-y'|}{|y|^2}
    $$
nodes.statement_short: Case $y'\le1<y$: reduce to the first case and use $y'\ge y/2$

nodes.name: Case $y,y'>1$: both values vanish
nodes.statement:
Finally, if $y, y' > 1$ then
    $$
        |\kappa(-y) - \kappa(-y')| = 0 \le 2^{8} \frac{|y-y'|}{|y|^2}\,.
    $$
nodes.statement_short: Case $y,y'>1$: both values vanish

nodes.name: Proof of convergence for $C^2$ functions
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to summable coefficients; two integrations by parts give $|\hat f_n|\lesssim n^{-2}$.
nodes.statement: By \Cref{convergence-of-coeffs-summable}, it suffices to show that the Fourier coefficients $\widehat{f}_n$ are summable. Applying \Cref{fourier-coeff-derivative} twice and using the fact that $f''$ is continuous and thus bounded on $[0,2\pi]$ , we compute \begin{equation*} \sum_{n\in {\mathbb{Z}}} |\widehat{f}_n| = |\widehat{f}_0| + \sum_{n\in {\mathbb{Z}} \setminus \{0\}} \frac {1}{n^2} |\widehat{f''}_n| \le |\widehat{f}_0| + \left(\sup_{x\in [0,2\pi]} |f(x)| \right) \cdot \sum_{n\in {\mathbb{Z}} \setminus \{0\}} \frac {1}{n^2} < \infty. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Proof of modulated averaged projection
nodes.statement_short: Modulations are $L^2$ isometries; triangle inequality and the spectral projection bound.
nodes.statement: We have \begin{equation} \|M_ng\|_{L^2[0, 2\pi]}^2=\int_{0}^{2\pi} |e^{inx}g(x)|^2\, dx =\int_{0}^{2\pi} |g(x)|^2\, dx=\|g\|_{L^2[0, 2\pi]}^2\, . \end{equation} We have by the triangle inequality, the square root of the identity in \eqref{mnbound}, and \Cref{spectral-projection-bound} \begin{equation*} \|L_ng\|_{L^2[0, 2\pi]}=\|\frac 1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} M_{n+N} S_{N+n}M_{-N-n}g\|_{L^2[0, 2\pi]} \end{equation*} \begin{equation*} \le \frac 1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \| M_{n+N} S_{N+n}M_{-N-n}g\|_{L^2[0, 2\pi]} = \frac 1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \| S_{N+n}M_{-N-n}g\|_{L^2[0, 2\pi]} \end{equation*} \begin{equation} \le \frac 1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \| M_{-N-n}g\|_{L^2[0, 2\pi]} = \frac 1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \| g\|_{L^2[0, 2\pi]} =\|g\|_{L^2[0, 2\pi]}\, . \end{equation} This proves \eqref{lnbound} and completes the proof of the lemma.

We have

nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a bounded $2\pi$-periodic function. We have for any $0 \le x\le 2\pi$ that \begin{equation} \int_0^{2\pi} f(y)\, dy= \int_{-x}^{2\pi -x} f(y)\, dy =\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(y-x)\, dy\,. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of periodic domain shift
nodes.statement_short: Periodicity and change of variables, then split the domain of integration.
nodes.statement: We have by periodicity and change of variables \begin{equation} \int_{-x}^{0} f(y)\, dy=\int_{-x}^{0} f(y+2\pi)\, dy= \int_{2\pi -x}^{2\pi} f(y)\, dy\, . \end{equation} We then have by breaking up the domain of integration and using \eqref{eqhil9} \begin{equation*} \int_0^{2\pi} f(y)\, dy= \int_0^{2\pi -x} f(y)\, dy+ \int_{2\pi -x}^{2\pi} f(y)\, dy \end{equation*} \begin{equation} = \int_0^{2\pi -x} f(y)\, dy+ \int_{ -x}^{0} f(y)\, dy = \int_{-x}^{2\pi-x} f(y)\, dy\, . \end{equation} This proves the first identity of the lemma. The second identity follows by substitution of $y$ by $y-x$.

nodes.statement: Let $f$ and $g$ be two bounded non-negative measurable $2\pi$-periodic functions on ${\mathbb{R}}$. Then \begin{equation} \left(\int_0^{2\pi} \left(\int_0^{2\pi} f(y)g(x-y)\, dy\right)^2\, dx\right)^{\frac 12}\le \|f\|_{L^2[0, 2\pi]} \|g\|_{L^1[0, 2\pi]}\, . \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of Young convolution
nodes.statement_short: Fubini with domain shift, then Cauchy-Schwarz after writing $g=h^2$.
nodes.statement: Using Fubini and \Cref{periodic-domain-shift}, we observe \begin{equation*} \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(y)^2g(x-y)\, dy \, dx=\int_0^{2\pi}f(y)^2\int_0^{2\pi}g(x-y)\, dx \, dy \end{equation*} \begin{equation} =\int_0^{2\pi}f(y)^2\int_0^{2\pi}g(x) \, dx dy =\|f\|_{L^2[0, 2\pi]}^2\|g\|_{L^1[0, 2\pi]}\, . \end{equation} Let $h$ be the nonnegative square root of $g$, then $h$ is bounded and $2\pi$-periodic with $h^2=g$. We estimate the square of the left-hand side of \eqref{eqyoung} with Cauchy-Schwarz and then with \eqref{eqhil4} by \begin{equation*} \int_0^{2\pi} (\int_0^{2\pi}f(y)h(x-y)h(x-y)\, dy)^2\, dx \end{equation*} \begin{equation*} \le \int_0^{2\pi}\left(\int_0^{2\pi}f(y)^2g(x-y)\, dy\right) \left(\int_0^{2\pi}g(x-y)\, dy\right)\, dx \end{equation*} \begin{equation*} = \|f\|_{L^2[0, 2\pi]}^2\|g\|_{L^1[0, 2\pi]}^2\, . \end{equation*} Taking square roots, this proves the lemma.

nodes.name: Proof of Hilbert strong 2 2
nodes.statement_short: Compare $H_r$ with $2\pi L_N$ on functions supported in short intervals using the Dirichlet approximation, then translate and sum over unit intervals.
nodes.statement: We first show that if $f$ is supported in $[1, 4]$, then \begin{equation} \|H_r f\|_{L^2[2, 3]} \le 2^{8} \|f\|_{L^2({\mathbb{R}})}\,. \end{equation} Let $\tilde{f}$ be the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $f$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Let $N$ be the smallest integer larger than $\frac 1r$. Then, \Cref{eqdifflhil} shows that the kernels of $H_r$ and $2\pi L_N$ differ by at most $12k_r$ on $[-\pi, \pi]$. Consider $x \in [2,3]$. When computing $H_r f(x)$ and $2\pi L_N f(x)$, the kernels are computed at points of the form $x-y$ with $f(y) \ne 0$, i.e., $y \in [1,4]$. As $x\in [2,3]$, the difference $x-y$ is bounded in absolute value by $2$, and therefore belongs to $[-\pi, \pi]$, where the above bound holds. It follows that, for $x \in [2,3]$, \begin{equation*} |H_r \tilde{f}(x)|\leq 2\pi |L_N \tilde{f}(x)|+12\left|\int_{0}^{2\pi}k_r(x-y)\tilde{f}(y)\, dy\right|. \end{equation*} Taking $L^2$ norm and using its sub-additivity, we get \begin{equation*} \|H_r \tilde{f}\|_{L^2[2, 3]}\leq 2\pi \|L_N \tilde{f}\|_{L^2[0, 2\pi]}\, + 12\left(\int_{0}^{2\pi} \left|\int_{0}^{2\pi}k_r(x-y)\tilde{f}(y)\, dy\right|^2\, dx\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}. \end{equation*} Since $\kappa$ is supported in $[-1,1]$, we have that $H_r\tilde{f}$ agrees with $H_r f$ on $[2,3]$. Using \Cref{modulated-averaged-projection} and \Cref{integrable-bump-convolution}, we conclude \begin{equation} \|H_r f\|_{L^2[2, 3]} \le 2\pi \|f\|_{L^2[0, 2\pi]} + 12 \cdot 17 \|f\|_{L^2[0, 2\pi]}\,, \end{equation} which gives \eqref{eq-Hr-short-support}. Suppose now that $f$ is supported in $[c, c+3]$ for some $c \in {\mathbb{R}}$. Then the function $g(x) = f(x-c+1)$ is supported in $[1, 4]$. By a change of variables in \eqref{def-H-r}, we have $H_r g(x ) = H_r f(x - c + 1)$. Thus, by \eqref{eq-Hr-short-support} \begin{equation} \|H_rf\|_{L^2[c+1, c+2]} = \|H_r g\|_{L^2[2,3]} \le 2^{8} \|g\|_2 = 2^8 \|f\|_2\,. \end{equation} Let now $f$ be arbitrary. Since $\kappa(x) = 0$ for $|x| > 1$, we have for all $x \in [c+1, c+2]$ $$ H_rf(x) = H_r(f \mathbf{1}_{[c, c+3]})(x)\,. $$ Thus $$ \int_{c+1}^{c+2} |H_r f(x)|^2 \, \mathrm{d}x = \int_{c+1}^{c+2}|H_r(f \mathbf{1}_{[c, c+3]})(x)|^2 \, \mathrm{d}x\,. $$ Applying the bound \eqref{eq-Hr-short-support-2}, this is $$ \le 2^{16} \int_{c}^{c+3} |f(x)|^2 \, \mathrm{d}x\,. $$ Summing over all $c \in \mathbb{Z}$, we obtain $$ \int_{{\mathbb{R}}} |H_rf(x)|^2 \, \mathrm{d}x \le 3 \cdot 2^{16} \int_{{\mathbb{R}}} |f(x)|^2 \, \mathrm{d}x\,. $$ This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Proof of van der Corput
nodes.statement_short: Trivial bound when $n=0$ or $\beta-\alpha<\pi/n$; otherwise shift by half a period $\pi/n$ and use the Lipschitz bound.
nodes.statement: Let $g$ be a Lipschitz continuous function as in the lemma. Assume first that $n=0$. Then \begin{equation*} \int_\alpha^\beta g(x) \, \mathrm{d}x \le |\beta - \alpha| \sup_{\alpha\le x\le \beta}|g(x)| \le |\beta-\alpha|\|g\|_{Lip(\alpha,\beta)}(1+|n||\beta-\alpha|)^{-1} \end{equation*} Assume now $n\ne 0$. Without loss of generality, we may assume $n>0$. We distinguish two cases. If $\beta-\alpha < \frac{\pi}{n}$, we have by the triangle inequality \begin{equation*} \left|\int_\alpha^\beta g(x) e^{inx} \, \mathrm{d}x\right| \le |\beta -\alpha| \sup_{x \in [\alpha,\beta]} |g(x)| \le 2\pi |\beta-\alpha|\|g\|_{Lip(\alpha,\beta)}(1+|n||\beta-\alpha|)^{-1} \,. \end{equation*} We turn to the case $\frac{\pi}{n} \le \beta-\alpha$. We have $$ e^{in(x + \pi/n)} = -e^{inx}\,. $$ Using this, we write $$ \int_\alpha^\beta g(x) e^{inx} \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{1}{2} \int_\alpha^\beta g(x) e^{inx} \, \mathrm{d}x - \frac{1}{2} \int_\alpha^\beta g(x) e^{in(x + \pi/n)}) \, \mathrm{d}x\,. $$ We split the first integral at $\alpha + \frac{\pi}{n}$ and the second one at $\beta - \frac{\pi}{n}$, and make a change of variables in the second part of the first integral to obtain $$ = \frac{1}{2} \int_{\alpha}^{\alpha + \frac{\pi}{n}} g(x) e^{inx} \, \mathrm{d}x - \frac{1}{2} \int_{\beta - \frac{\pi}{n}}^{\beta} g(x) e^{in(x + \pi/n)} \, \mathrm{d}x $$ $$ + \frac{1}{2} \int_{\alpha + \frac{\pi}{n}}^{\beta} (g(x) - g(x - \frac{\pi}{n})) e^{inx} \, \mathrm{d}x\,. $$ The sum of the first two terms is by the triangle inequality bounded by $$ \frac{\pi}{n} \sup_{x \in [\alpha,\beta]} |g(x)|\,. $$ The third term is by the triangle inequality at most $$ \frac{1}{2} \int_{\alpha + \frac{\pi}{n}}^\beta |g(x) - g(x - \frac{\pi}{n})| \, \mathrm{d}x $$ $$ \le \frac{|\beta-\alpha|}{2} \frac{\pi}{n} \sup_{\alpha \le x < y \le \beta} \frac{|g(x) - g(y)|}{|x-y|}\,. $$ Adding the two terms, we obtain $$ \left|\int_\alpha^\beta g(x) e^{-inx} \, \mathrm{d}x\right| \le \frac{\pi}{n} \|g\|_{\mathrm{Lip}(\alpha,\beta)}\,. $$ This completes the proof of the lemma, using that with $\frac{\pi}{n} \le \beta-\alpha$, $$ \frac{\pi}{n} = \frac{2 \pi |\beta-\alpha|}{2n|\beta-\alpha|} \le 2 \pi |\beta-\alpha|(1 + n|\beta-\alpha|)^{-1}\,. $$

nodes.name: Case $n\ne0$
nodes.statement:
Assume now $n\ne 0$. Without loss of generality, we may assume $n>0$.
We distinguish two cases. If $\beta-\alpha < \frac{\pi}{n}$, we have by the triangle inequality
\begin{equation*}
    \left|\int_\alpha^\beta g(x) e^{inx} \, \mathrm{d}x\right|
    \le |\beta -\alpha| \sup_{x \in [\alpha,\beta]} |g(x)|
    \le 2\pi |\beta-\alpha|\|g\|_{Lip(\alpha,\beta)}(1+|n||\beta-\alpha|)^{-1} \,.
\end{equation*}
We turn to the case $\frac{\pi}{n} \le \beta-\alpha$.
We have
$$
    e^{in(x + \pi/n)} = -e^{inx}\,.
$$
Using this, we write
$$
    \int_\alpha^\beta g(x) e^{inx} \, \mathrm{d}x
    = \frac{1}{2} \int_\alpha^\beta g(x) e^{inx} \, \mathrm{d}x - \frac{1}{2} \int_\alpha^\beta g(x) e^{in(x + \pi/n)}) \, \mathrm{d}x\,.
$$
We split the first integral at $\alpha + \frac{\pi}{n}$ and the second one at $\beta - \frac{\pi}{n}$, and make a change of variables in the second part of the first integral to obtain
$$
    = \frac{1}{2} \int_{\alpha}^{\alpha + \frac{\pi}{n}} g(x) e^{inx} \, \mathrm{d}x - \frac{1}{2} \int_{\beta - \frac{\pi}{n}}^{\beta} g(x) e^{in(x + \pi/n)} \, \mathrm{d}x
$$
$$
    + \frac{1}{2} \int_{\alpha + \frac{\pi}{n}}^{\beta} (g(x) - g(x - \frac{\pi}{n})) e^{inx} \, \mathrm{d}x\,.
$$
The sum of the first two terms is by the triangle inequality bounded by
$$
    \frac{\pi}{n} \sup_{x \in [\alpha,\beta]} |g(x)|\,.
$$
The third term is by the triangle inequality at most
$$
    \frac{1}{2} \int_{\alpha + \frac{\pi}{n}}^\beta |g(x) - g(x - \frac{\pi}{n})| \, \mathrm{d}x
$$
$$
    \le \frac{|\beta-\alpha|}{2} \frac{\pi}{n} \sup_{\alpha \le x < y \le \beta} \frac{|g(x) - g(y)|}{|x-y|}\,.
$$
Adding the two terms, we obtain
$$
    \left|\int_\alpha^\beta g(x) e^{-inx} \, \mathrm{d}x\right| \le \frac{\pi}{n} \|g\|_{\mathrm{Lip}(\alpha,\beta)}\,.
$$
This completes the proof of the lemma, using that with $\frac{\pi}{n} \le \beta-\alpha$,
$$
    \frac{\pi}{n} = \frac{2 \pi |\beta-\alpha|}{2n|\beta-\alpha|} \le 2 \pi |\beta-\alpha|(1 + n|\beta-\alpha|)^{-1}\,.
$$

nodes.statement_short: Orthonormality of $e^{inx}$ (Parseval/Bessel) bounds the norm of the partial sum.
nodes.statement: The functions $e_n:x\mapsto e^{inx}$ form an orthonormal basis in $L^2[-\pi, \pi]$ (this is already in Mathlib). Therefore we have \begin{align*} \|S_Nf\|^2_{L^2[-\pi, \pi]} &= \|\sum_{n=-N}^N \langle\widehat{f}_n, e_n\rangle_{L^2[-\pi, \pi]}\|^2_{L^2[-\pi, \pi]} \\ &= \sum_{n=-N}^N |\widehat{f}_n| \\ &\le \sum_{n\in \mathbb{Z}} |\widehat{f}_n| \\ &= \|f\|_{L^2[-\pi, \pi]}. \end{align*} This completes the proof of the lemma.

nodes.name: Dirichlet kernel - Hilbert kernel relation
nodes.statement_short: The Dirichlet kernel equals two modulated Hilbert kernels up to a bounded error $\pi$.
nodes.statement: For all $N\in{\mathbb{Z}}$ and $x\in [-\pi,\pi] \setminus \{0\}$, \begin{equation*} \left|K_N(x) - (e^{-iNx}\kappa(x) + \overline{e^{-iNx}\kappa(x)})\right| \le \pi \,. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Proof of Dirichlet kernel - Hilbert kernel relation
nodes.statement_short: Closed form of $K_N$ and the lower secant bound with $\eta=\min(|x|,1)$.
nodes.statement: Let $N\in{\mathbb{Z}}$ and $x\in [-\pi,\pi] \setminus \{0\}$. With \Cref{Dirichlet-kernel}, we obtain \begin{equation*} K_N(x) - (e^{-iNx}\kappa(x) + \overline{e^{-iNx}\kappa(x)}) = e^{-iNx} \frac{\min(|x|, 1) }{1 - e^{ix}} + e^{iNx} \frac{\min(|x|, 1) }{1 - e^{-ix}} \,. \end{equation*} Using \Cref{lower-secant-bound} with $\eta = \min(|x|, 1)$, we bound \begin{equation*} \left|K_N(x) - (e^{-iNx}\kappa(x) + \overline{e^{-iNx}\kappa(x)})\right| \le \frac{\min(|x|, 1) }{|1 - e^{ix}|} + \frac{\min(|x|, 1)}{|1 - e^{-ix}|} \le \frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{2} = \pi \,. \end{equation*}

nodes.statement_short: Partial Fourier sums of a bounded $g$ are controlled by the Carleson operator of $g,\bar g$ plus $\pi\delta$.
nodes.statement: Let $g:{\mathbb{R}}\to\mathbb{C}$ be a measurable $2\pi$-periodic function such that for some $\delta>0$ and every $x\in{\mathbb{R}}$, \begin{equation} |g(x)|\le \delta \,. \end{equation} Then for every $x\in [0,2\pi]$ and $N>0$, \begin{equation*} |S_N g(x)| \le \frac{1}{2\pi} (Tg(x) + T\bar{g}(x)) + \pi\delta. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Proof of partial Fourier sum bound
nodes.statement_short: Write $S_Ng$ via the Dirichlet kernel, split off the bounded difference from modulated Hilbert kernels, and bound the singular part by $T$.
nodes.statement: Let $x\in [0,2\pi]$ and $N>0$. We have with \Cref{Dirichlet-kernel} \begin{equation*} |S_N g(x)| = \frac{1}{2\pi} \left| \int_0^{2\pi} g(y) K_N(x-y) \, dy\right|\,. \end{equation*} We use $2\pi$-periodicity of $g$ and $K_N$ to shift the domain of integration to obtain \begin{equation*} = \frac{1}{2\pi} \left|\int_{x-\pi}^{x+\pi} g(y) K_N(x-y) \, dy\right|\,. \end{equation*} Using the triangle inequality, we split this as \begin{equation} \le \frac{1}{2\pi} \left|\int_{x-\pi}^{x+\pi} g(y) \left(K_N(x-y) - \max(|x-y|,0) K_N(x-y)\right) \, dy \right| \end{equation} \begin{equation} + \frac{1}{2\pi} \left|\int_{x-\pi}^{x+\pi} g(y) \max(|x-y|,0) K_N(x-y) \, dy\right|\,. \end{equation} Note that all integrals are well defined, since $K_N$ is by \eqref{eqksumexp} bounded by $2N+1$. Using that \begin{equation} \max(|x-y|,0) K_N(x-y) = e^{-iN(x-y)}\kappa(x-y) + \overline{e^{-iN(x-y)}\kappa(x-y)} \,, \end{equation} \Cref{Dirichlet-Hilbert} and \eqref{g-small}, we bound \eqref{eq-diff-integrable} by \begin{equation*} \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{x-\pi}^{x+\pi} |g(y)| \left|K_N(x-y) - e^{-iN(x-y)}\kappa(x-y) + \overline{e^{-iN(x-y)}\kappa(x-y)}\right|\, dy \le \pi\delta \,. \end{equation*} By dominated convergence and since $\kappa(x-y) = 0$ for $|x-y| > 1$, \eqref{eq-diff-singular} equals \begin{equation*} \frac{1}{2\pi} \lim_{r \to 0^+} \left| \int_{r < |x-y| < 1} g(y) \max(|x-y|,0) K_N(x-y) \, dy\right|\,. \end{equation*} We bound the limit by a supremum and rewrite using \eqref{eq-Dirichlet-Hilbert}, \begin{equation*} \le \frac{1}{2\pi} \sup_{r > 0} \left| \int_{r < |x-y| < 1} g(y) \left(e^{-iN(x-y)}\kappa(x-y) + \overline{e^{-iN(x-y)}\kappa(x-y)}\right) \, dy\right| \end{equation*} Using the triangle inequality, we further bound this by \begin{alignat*}{3} \le&&&\frac{1}{2\pi} \sup_{r > 0} \left| \int_{r < |x-y| < 1} g(y) e^{-iNy} \kappa(x-y) \, dy\right| \\ &+ &&\frac{1}{2\pi} \sup_{r > 0} \left| \int_{r < |x-y| < 1} \overline{g}(y) e^{-iNy} \kappa(x-y) \, dy\right|\,. \end{alignat*} By the definition \eqref{define-T-carleson} of $T$, this is \begin{equation*} \le \frac{1}{2\pi} (Tg(x) + T\bar{g}(x))\,. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Proof of real Carleson operator measurable
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to countable suprema using continuity in $r$, then measurability of the integrand in $(x,y)$.
nodes.statement: Since a countable supremum of measurable functions is measurable, it suffices to show that for every $n\in{\mathbb{Z}}$, \begin{equation*} x \mapsto \sup_{r>0}\left|\int_{r<|x-y|<1} f(y)\kappa(x-y) e^{iny}\, dy\right| \end{equation*} is measurable. So let $n\in{\mathbb{Z}}$. Note that for each $x\in{\mathbb{R}}$, the function \begin{equation*} r \mapsto \left|\int_{r<|x-y|<1} f(y)\kappa(x-y) e^{iny}\, dy\right| \end{equation*} is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ since the integrand is locally bounded on the domain $0<|x-y|<1$ by the assumptions on $f$ and \Cref{Hilbert-kernel-bound}. Thus, for each $x\in{\mathbb{R}}$, \begin{equation*} \sup_{r>0}\left|\int_{r<|x-y|<1} f(y)\kappa(x-y) e^{iny}\, dy\right| =\sup_{r\in{\mathbb{Q}}_{>0}}\left|\int_{r<|x-y|<1} f(y)\kappa(x-y) e^{iny}\, dy\right| \end{equation*} The right hand side is again a countable supremum so it remains to show that for every $r\in{\mathbb{Q}}_{>0}$, \begin{equation*} x \mapsto \left|\int_{r<|x-y|<1} f(y)\kappa(x-y) e^{iny}\, dy\right| = \left|\int \mathbf{1}_{\{r<|x-\cdot|<1\}}(y) f(y)\kappa(x-y) e^{iny}\, dy\right| \end{equation*} is measurable, which follows from the fact that the integrand is measurable in $(x,y)$.

nodes.name: partial Fourier sums of small
conclusions: there exists a measurable set $E\subset [0,2\pi]$ with $|E|<\epsilon$
nodes.statement_short: Partial Fourier sums of a $\delta$-small $g$ are at most $C_\epsilon\delta$ outside a set of measure $<\epsilon$.
nodes.statement: Let $g:{\mathbb{R}}\to\mathbb{C}$ be a measurable $2\pi$-periodic function such that for some $\delta>0$ and every $x\in{\mathbb{R}}$, \begin{equation} |g(x)|\le \delta \,. \end{equation} Then for every $\epsilon>0$, there exists a measurable set $E\subset [0,2\pi]$ with $|E|<\epsilon$ such that for every $x\in [0,2\pi]\setminus E$ and $N>0$, \begin{equation} |S_N g(x)|\le C_\epsilon \delta, \end{equation} where \begin{equation} C_\epsilon = \left(\frac{8}{\pi\epsilon}\right)^\frac{1}{2} C_{4,2} + \pi \,. \end{equation}
nodes.label: partial-Fourier-sums-of-small

nodes.name: Smallness of $g$

nodes.label: g-small

nodes.name: Small partial sums
nodes.statement: |S_N g(x)|\le C_\epsilon \delta,
nodes.label: S-Ng-small

nodes.name: Constant $C_\epsilon$
nodes.statement: C_\epsilon = \left(\frac{8}{\pi\epsilon}\right)^\frac{1}{2} C_{4,2} + \pi \,.
nodes.label: C-epsilon-def

nodes.name: Proof of partial Fourier sums of small
nodes.statement_short: Define the exceptional set by the maximal partial sum; cover it by two level sets of $T$ and bound each with real Carleson.
nodes.statement: Define \begin{equation*} E := \{x \in [0, 2\pi] \ : \ \sup_{N > 0} |S_N g (x)| > C_\epsilon \delta \} \,. \end{equation*} Then \eqref{S-Ng-small} clearly holds, and it remains to show that $|E| \le \epsilon$. With \Cref{partial-Fourier-sum-bound}, we obtain \begin{equation*} E \subset \{x\in [0,2\pi] \ : \ C_\epsilon \delta < \frac{1}{2\pi} (Tg(x) + T\bar{g}(x)) + \pi\delta\} \subset E_1 \cup E_2, \end{equation*} where \begin{align*} E_1 :=& \{x\in [0,2\pi] \ : \ \pi(C_\epsilon - \pi) \delta < Tg(x)\} \\ E_2 :=& \{x\in [0,2\pi] \ : \ \pi(C_\epsilon - \pi) \delta < T\bar{g}(x)\}. \end{align*} By \Cref{real-Carleson-operator-measurable}, $E_1$ and $E_2$ are measurable. Thus, \begin{equation*} \pi(C_\epsilon - \pi) \delta |E_1| \le \int_{E_1} Tg(x) \, dx = \delta \int_{E_1} T(\delta^{-1} g\mathbf{1}_{[-\pi,3\pi]})(x) \, dx \,. \end{equation*} Applying \Cref{real-Carleson} with $F = [-\pi, 3\pi]$ and $G = E'$, it follows that this is \begin{equation*} \le \delta \cdot C_{4,2} |F|^{\frac{1}{2}} |E_1|^{\frac{1}{2}} \le (4\pi)^\frac{1}{2} C_{4,2} \delta \cdot |E'|^{\frac{1}{2}}\,. \end{equation*} Rearranging, we obtain \begin{equation*} |E_1| \le \left(\frac{(4\pi)^\frac{1}{2} C_{4,2}}{\pi(C_\epsilon - \pi)}\right)^2 = \frac{\epsilon}{2}\,. \end{equation*} Analogously, we get the same estimate for $|E_2|$. This completes the proof using $|E| \le |E_1| + |E_2|$.

nodes.name: Proof of real line ball
nodes.statement_short: Unfold $|x'-x|<R$ into two inequalities, in both directions.
nodes.statement: Let $x'\in B(x,R)$. By definition of the ball, $|x'-x|<R$. It follows that $x'-x<R$ and $x-x'<R$. It follows $x'<x+R$ and $x'>x-R$. This implies $x'\in (x-R,x+R)$. Conversely, let $x'\in (x-R,x+R)$. Then $x'<x+R$ and $x'>x-R$. It follows that $x'-x<R$ and $x-x'<R$. It follows that $|x'-x|<R$, hence $x'\in B(x,R)$. This proves the lemma.

nodes.name: Proof of integer ball cover
nodes.statement_short: Choose centers $n\pm R'/(2R)$ rounded and $n$; check membership by cases on $n'$.
nodes.statement: Let $m_1$ be the largest integer smaller than or equal to $n- \frac {R'} {2R}$. Let $m_2=n$. Let $m_3$ be the smallest integer larger than or equal to $n+ \frac {R'} {2R}$. Let ${\vartheta}_{n'}\in B'$, then with \eqref{eqcarl4}, we have \begin{equation} 2R|n-n'|< 2R'\, . \end{equation} Assume first $n'\le m_1$. With \eqref{eqcarl6} we have \begin{equation*} R|m_1-n'|=R(m_1-n')=R(m_1-n)+R(n-n') \end{equation*} \begin{equation} < -\frac{R'}2+R'=-\frac{R'}2\, . \end{equation} We conclude ${\vartheta}_{n'}\in B_1$. Assume next $m_1<n'<m_3$. Then ${\vartheta}_{n'}\in B_2$. Assume finally that $m_3\le n'$. With \eqref{eqcarl6} we have \begin{equation*} R|m_3-n'|=R(n'-m_3)=R(n'-n)+R(n-m_3) \end{equation*} \begin{equation} < R' -\frac{R'}2=-\frac{R'}2\, . \end{equation} We conclude ${\vartheta}_{n'}\in B_1$. This completes the proof of the lemma.

nodes.name: Proof of real Carleson

nodes.statement: The preceding chain of lemmas establishes that ${\Theta}$ is a cancellative, compatible collection of functions on $({\mathbb{R}}, \rho, \mu, 4)$. Again, some of the statements in these lemmas are stronger than what is needed for $a=4$, but can be relaxed to give the desired conclusion for $a=4$. With $\kappa$ as near \eqref{eq-hilker}, define the function $K:{\mathbb{R}}\times {\mathbb{R}}\to \mathbb{C}$ as in Theorem \ref{metric-space-Carleson} by \begin{equation} K(x,y):=\kappa(x-y)\, . \end{equation} The function $K$ is continuous outside the diagonal $x=y$ and vanishes on the diagonal. Hence it is measurable. By \Cref{Hilbert-kernel-bound,Hilbert-kernel-regularity}, it follows that $K$ is a two-sided Calder\'on--Zygmund kernel on $({\mathbb{R}},\rho,\mu,4)$. \Cref{Hilbert-strong-2-2} verifies \eqref{two-sided-Hr-bound-assumption}. Thus the assumptions of \Cref{two-sided-metric-space-Carleson} are all satisfied. Applying the Theorem, \Cref{real-Carleson} follows.
